masked_text: The court dismissed Plaintiffs' FHA claims under § 3604(b) and § 3617 because the complaint lacked sufficient factual allegations to plausibly establish that Defendant's actions were motivated by [CLASS] discrimination rather than legitimate concerns about the party size and conduct. Plaintiffs John and Alberta Dogbe, who are of African descent, sued their landlord The Lakes at Lemmon Valley, LLC alleging [CLASS] discrimination after being required to end a clubhouse party and receiving an eviction notice. The court granted Defendant's motion to dismiss the FHA claims, finding the complaint lacked sufficient factual allegations to plausibly allege discrimination because of [CLASS], though the court granted leave to amend. Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege that [CLASS] was a motivating factor in Defendant's decision to shut down the party and serve an eviction notice. The complaint contains only speculation and conclusory statements that the conduct was [CLASS]-based, without factual allegations comparing treatment of similarly situated non-African individuals or explaining why guests believed [CLASS] prejudice motivated the conduct. 12(b)(6) Plaintiffs did not plausibly allege that Defendant interfered with their right to enjoy their apartment free from [CLASS] discrimination under § 3617. The allegations do not support the conclusion that Defendant took action against Plaintiffs (serving the eviction notice) because of their [CLASS]. 12(b)(6) Sections 1981 and 1982 claims failed because Plaintiffs did not plausibly allege [CLASS] was a but-for cause of the injury. Nevada fair housing law claim failed for the same reasons as the FHA claim. Constructive eviction claim failed due to insufficient factual allegations. Breach of implied covenant claim lacked factual specificity. Unjust enrichment claim was barred by the existence of an express written lease. IIED claim failed because the alleged conduct was not extreme and outrageous. NIED claim failed because Plaintiffs did not assert an underlying negligence claim. 12(b)(6)

row_id: RACE-DT|10299511_2024_Clark v. GSL Properties, Inc._ord
case_name: Brooklynn C. Clark v. GSL Properties, Inc. et al.
masked_text: Plaintiff fails to state an FHA claim because she did not allege the [CLASS], sex, or gender identity of her neighbors to establish that similarly situated individuals outside her protected class were treated more favorably. Brooklynn Clark, a [CLASS] transgender woman with anxiety, sued GSL Properties Inc. and related defendants alleging discrimination during her tenancy including disproportionate rent increases, police contact, and eviction. The court recommends dismissing her FHA claims because she failed to adequately plead that similarly situated individuals outside her protected classes were treated more favorably, and recommends dismissal of her ADA and Title VII claims on separate grounds. The court did not reach the merits of the [CLAIM] claims. The court dismissed the amended complaint under § 1915(e)(2)(B) screening for failure to state a plausible FHA claim, applying Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards. The court found that Clark failed to allege facts sufficient to support her FHA claims based on [CLASS] and sex discrimination, and did not separately analyze whether the requested accommodations were reasonable or whether defendants engaged in the interactive process. Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B) Clark failed to allege that similarly situated individuals outside her protected class were treated more favorably. Although she alleged that neighbors paid less rent, she did not allege the [CLASS], sex, or gender identity of those neighbors, and thus failed to plausibly allege [CLAIM] based on a protected status under the Iqbal/Twombly standard. Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B) The court dismissed Clark's FHA claims (including any retaliation theory under § 3617) for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly. The court found that Clark did not allege facts suggesting that the negative treatment and eviction were because of a protected status, and did not separately analyze the retaliation claim on its merits. Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B) The court dismissed the ADA claims because Clark did not allege that defendants were a public entity (Title II) or operated a place of public [CLAIM] (Title III), and residential apartment complexes are not covered by the ADA. The court dismissed the Title VII claim because Clark did not allege that any defendants were her employer, that she suffered an adverse employment action, or that defendants treated other employees more favorably. Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B) and lack of applicability

masked_text: The court dismissed the case for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction because there was no diversity of citizenship (both parties are Texas citizens) and no federal question jurisdiction, as plaintiff failed to plead facts showing a plausible Fair Housing Act violation even under liberal construction of her [CLASS] and age discrimination claims. Pro se plaintiff Linda Kay Holloway sued Delia SiFuentes alleging [CLASS] and age discrimination after a failed real estate transaction where SiFuentes, a real estate agent Holloway had contacted to help purchase her rented home, ultimately purchased the property herself. The magistrate judge recommended dismissing the case without prejudice for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, finding no diversity of citizenship and that even liberally construed, Holloway's complaint failed to state plausible facts supporting a Fair Housing Act violation. Court liberally construed pro se plaintiff's allegations as raising a Fair Housing Act [CLAIM] claim based on [CLASS] and age discrimination in a real estate transaction, but dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction because plaintiff failed to allege facts plausibly showing discrimination by the real estate agent, and the claim was not properly pleaded to establish federal question jurisdiction. 12(b)(1) Court dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1332 because plaintiff and defendant are both Texas citizens (no diversity) and the breach of fiduciary duty claim arises under state law (no federal question). 12(b)(1)

row_id: RACE-DT|10305742_2024_Johnson-Byrd v. PennyMac Loan Services, LLC_mowd
case_name: Arlene Johnson-Byrd, et al. v. PennyMac Loan Services, LLC
masked_text: The court granted PennyMac's motion to dismiss all of Johnson-Byrd's claims on res judicata grounds, holding that the state court's dismissal without prejudice became a final judgment on the merits when Johnson-Byrd elected not to refile in state court, and alternatively dismissing counts 1–4 for failure to state a claim. Plaintiff Arlene Johnson-Byrd sued PennyMac Loan Services asserting [CLASS] discrimination (42 U.S.C. § 1981), FHA discrimination in residential lending (§ 3605), FHA interference (§ 3617), fraudulent misrepresentation, breach of contract, and Missouri Merchandising Practices Act violations, all arising from PennyMac's alleged mishandling of escrow funds under her rehabilitation mortgage loan. The court dismissed co-plaintiff Louis Byrd for lack of standing because he was not a party to the loan contract, then dismissed all of Johnson-Byrd's claims under res judicata, reasoning that the state court's prior dismissal without prejudice—entered as a discovery sanction—ripened into a final judgment on the merits when Johnson-Byrd failed to refile in state court. As an alternative basis, the court dismissed Count 1 (§ 1981) for conclusory pleading of discriminatory intent, Counts 2 and 3 as time-barred under the FHA's two-year limitations period, and Count 4 (fraud) under the economic loss doctrine. Count 2 alleges discrimination under § 3605 based on PennyMac's refusal to release escrow funds. The alleged discriminatory conduct ended in September 2021 when plaintiff sold the property. The complaint was filed March 20, 2024, nearly three years later, exceeding the two-year statute of limitations under 42 U.S.C. § 3613. 12(b)(6) Count 3 alleges interference under § 3617 based on misconduct during the rehabilitation project. All conduct ended in September 2021. The complaint was filed March 20, 2024, nearly three years later, exceeding the two-year statute of limitations under 42 U.S.C. § 3613. 12(b)(6) All claims are barred by res judicata because: (1) the prior state court judgment was rendered by a court of competent jurisdiction; (2) the state court's dismissal without prejudice became a final judgment on the merits when plaintiff failed to refile in state court as required; and (3) the same cause of action (PennyMac's alleged mismanagement of the loan) and parties are involved in both cases. The nucleus of operative facts is identical. 12(b)(6)

row_id: RACE-DT|10355743_2025_Reyes v. Harris County_txsd
case_name: Art Reyes v. Harris County, Christopher Ross, Amanda Fry, Alexzander French Michael, and Joseph M. Douglass
masked_text: The court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA claim because he failed to allege that Harris County discriminated in the sale or rental of housing, real estate transactions, brokerage services, or otherwise coerced, intimidated, or interfered with his fair housing rights under 42 U.S.C. §§ 3604, 3605, 3606, or 3617. Art Reyes, proceeding pro se, sued Harris County and individual deputies under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and the Fair Housing Act, alleging that deputies discriminated against him based on [CLASS] by repeatedly detaining, arresting, and charging him while declining to arrest his [CLASS] neighbors for similar conduct. The court granted Harris County's motion to dismiss, dismissing all claims because Plaintiff failed to adequately plead a Monell claim against the County and because his FHA claim fell outside the statute's scope as he alleged police misconduct rather than discrimination in housing transactions. The court held that the FHA claim failed because Harris County did not engage in prohibited conduct under the Act. The FHA prohibits discrimination in the sale or rental of housing, real estate transactions, brokerage services, and coercion/intimidation related to those activities. Plaintiff failed to allege that Harris County discriminated in any of these contexts; instead, he alleged that deputies prevented access to common amenities, which does not fall within the scope of FHA-prohibited conduct under §§ 3604, 3605, 3606, or 3617. 12(b)(6) Harris County failed to state a cognizable § 1983 claim against the municipal defendant because Plaintiff failed to allege facts supporting any of the three required Monell elements: a policymaker, an official policy, and a causal connection between that policy and the alleged constitutional violations. Plaintiff merely named Harris County as the employer of the deputies without alleging municipal policy or custom. Texas Penal Code claims were dismissed because the Texas Penal Code does not create private causes of action. 12(b)(6)

masked_text: The court granted the motion to dismiss all claims, finding that plaintiff's § 1983 false arrest, malicious prosecution, equal protection, and double jeopardy claims each failed to satisfy their required elements, and that plaintiff's FHA claim failed because the deputies' conduct—interfering with access to HOA common amenities—did not fall within the FHA's prohibitions on discrimination in housing sales, rentals, real estate transactions, or brokerage services. The court dismissed all § 1983 claims, finding the false arrest claims defeated by probable cause, the malicious prosecution claims deficient for lack of unlawful seizure and malice, the equal protection claim unsupported because Reyes failed to identify similarly situated comparators outside his protected class who were treated more favorably, and the double jeopardy claim inapplicable because the three charges arose from three discrete incidents. The FHA claim was dismissed because none of the FHA's enumerated provisions—covering discrimination in housing sales/rentals, real estate transactions, brokerage services, or interference with rights thereunder—applied to law enforcement conduct affecting access to HOA amenities. All § 1983 claims dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly. False arrest claims lack probable cause allegations; malicious prosecution claims fail threshold element of unlawful seizure and lack malice allegations; equal protection claim fails to allege similarly situated comparators outside protected class; double jeopardy claim fails because three arrests stemmed from three discrete criminal acts. 12(b)(6) FHA claim dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege that defendants discriminated in sale or rental of housing, real estate transactions, brokerage services, or otherwise coerced, intimidated, or interfered with rights secured by §§ 3604, 3605, 3606, or 3617. The FHA sections cited are wholly inapplicable to plaintiff's allegations regarding access to community amenities. 12(b)(6)

row_id: RACE-DT|10619198_2025_Arocho v. Chicopee Housing Authority_mad
case_name: Arocho v. Chicopee Housing Authority
masked_text: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA claims because they failed to plead facts showing they were personally subjected to discriminatory conduct, failed to identify similarly situated comparators treated differently based on [CLASS], and because the claims were barred by the FHA's two-year statute of limitations. Relatives and visitors of a murder victim sued the Chicopee Housing Authority and its executive director, claiming the housing authority violated the FHA by failing to evict a violent tenant with a known criminal history while making derogatory comments about [CLASS] residents, thereby discriminating based on [CLASS] and national origin. The state-created danger exception does not apply because the plaintiffs did not allege an affirmative act by defendants that increased the threat of third-party harm; merely relocating Urimagua-Guraboa next to Laracuente is an allegation of rendering her more vulnerable to risk, not an affirmative act. row_id: RACE-DT|10647541_2025_Montgomery, Jr. - Adams-II v. Anderson_laed
case_name: Cindy Adams v. Consuelleo Anderson, et al.
masked_text: The court granted HUD's motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(1) because plaintiff failed to establish subject matter jurisdiction over her claims against HUD, as sovereign immunity bars suits against federal agencies absent an express waiver, and plaintiff did not identify any applicable waiver for her discrimination, tort, or other claims. Plaintiff Cindy Adams, who alleges she lived in HUD-owned public housing, sued HUD along with nineteen other defendants asserting [CLASS] discrimination, premise liability, civil rights, and tort claims. The court granted HUD's motion to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding that sovereign immunity bars plaintiff's claims against HUD because she failed to identify any statutory waiver of sovereign immunity applicable to her claims for money damages, including under the Fair Housing Act. The United States and its agencies are shielded by sovereign immunity absent an express waiver. Plaintiff failed to identify any applicable waiver of sovereign immunity. Section 1983 does not apply to federal officials; the FHA does not waive sovereign immunity for money damages against the federal government; Title VI does not waive sovereign immunity; Tucker Act claims must be brought in the Court of Federal Claims; and FTCA claims require administrative exhaustion, which plaintiff failed to satisfy as evidenced by unrebutted HUD records showing no claims filed for injury or damages. 12(b)(1)

masked_text: The § 3604(b) [CLASS] discrimination claim survived against Goncharko/5120 based on allegations of using a [CLASS] slur, disparate maintenance denial, and targeted eviction, but Coldwell Banker was dismissed for failure to plead [CLASS] motivation; the § 3604(f) [CLAIM] claim failed because requests for repairs are modifications, not accommodations under § 3604(f)(3)(B), and the § 3617 retaliation claim failed for lack of alleged protected activity. Steven Hobbs, a [CLASS] commercial mortgage broker and Chicago tenant, sued property owners Igor Goncharko and 5120 South LLC, property management company Coldwell Banker, and prior owner The Stewardship Group, alleging [CLASS] discrimination, [CLASS] discrimination, and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act, plus a § 1981 breach of contract claim related to an alleged purchase agreement for affordable housing. The court denied Goncharko/5120's motion to dismiss the § 3604(b) [CLASS] discrimination claim based on allegations of a [CLASS] slur, disparate maintenance, and targeted eviction, but dismissed Coldwell Banker entirely for failure to plead [CLASS] motive, dismissed the § 3604(f) [CLASS] [CLAIM] claim because repair requests are modifications not accommodations, and dismissed the § 3617 retaliation claim for failure to allege protected activity. Plaintiff failed to plead facts sufficient to infer that [CLASS] was a motivating factor in Coldwell Banker's conduct. The complaint alleges only that Coldwell Banker facilitated a lease without disclosing ERAMP terms and charged $2,000/month rent, but does not allege that Coldwell Banker disclosed ERAMP terms to non-[CLASS] individuals, charged them less, or targeted plaintiff because of his [CLASS]. Coldwell Banker's role as an upstream real estate broker does not establish plausible liability for discrimination attributed to the landlord after the lease was signed. 12(b)(6) Plaintiff's § 3604(b) claim against Goncharko/5120 survives dismissal. Plaintiff alleges sufficient facts to infer [CLASS] discrimination: refusal of maintenance services while providing them to non-[CLASS] tenants, use of [CLASS] slurs, discriminatory eviction, denial of insurance information, and overcharging rent. These allegations parallel Mehta v. Beaconridge, where similar facts survived dismissal. Plaintiff need not plead specific dates or explain how each action establishes discrimination at the pleading stage. 12(b)(6) Plaintiff failed to plead a cognizable [CLAIM] claim. Reasonable accommodations under § 3604(f) refer to 'rules, policies, practices, or services' necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling. Requests for construction or repair are more appropriately characterized as requests for reasonable modifications, which a landlord need only permit the tenant to make at the tenant's own expense, not as accommodations. The Seventh Circuit recognizes examples of accommodations as zoning ordinances, parking restrictions, and no-pets policies—not unit maintenance. 12(b)(6) Plaintiff's § 3604(f) [CLAIM] claim fails because the allegation that he was 'targeted for eviction despite his condition' does not establish purposeful discrimination. Purposeful discrimination requires that a decisionmaker undertake a course of action 'because of,' not merely 'in spite of,' the action's adverse effects on an identifiable group. Additionally, the allegation is inconsistent with the facts alleged, since eviction proceedings began before the spinal injury occurred. 12(b)(6) Plaintiff failed to allege that he engaged in protected activity under § 3617. Although plaintiff alleges that Goncharko/5120 retaliated by pursuing eviction, refusing maintenance, and withholding insurance information in response to requests for repairs and pursuit of unpaid lien funds, plaintiff does not allege that either activity occurred in an FHA context. Plaintiff did not allege that he previously complained to the property owner or housing authority that the maintenance refusals were discriminatory, nor that he sought the unpaid funds pursuant to his FHA rights. Coldwell Banker's role predates the [CLASS] and the alleged retaliatory conduct. 12(b)(6) Only The Stewardship Group was party to the purchase agreement and capable of breaching it. Non-parties Coldwell Banker, Goncharko, and 5120 South cannot be sued for breach of contract simply because they have a close relationship with the breaching party. Absent allegations of tortious interference, these defendants are improper defendants for a § 1981 breach of contract claim. 12(b)(6) Coldwell Banker's motion to dismiss the § 3604(f) [CLASS] discrimination claim is granted because the alleged misconduct—requested repairs and targeted eviction—are landlord-specific and the complaint pleads no facts tying Coldwell Banker to either. Coldwell Banker's role in the transaction predates the [CLASS], making any causal connection implausible. 12(b)(6)

The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding Parker failed to plead sufficient facts supporting a plausible inference that [CLASS] or sex motivated the allegedly discriminatory lease renewal offer or that he engaged in protected activity for the retaliation claim. Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege he engaged in protected activity under the FHA. While he filed PCHR complaints, he did not specify what they were for, and they appear to have concerned housing code violations rather than discriminatory housing practices, which do not constitute protected activity under § 3617. 12(b)(6) Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege [CLAIM] based on sex. His allegations that defendants allowed nonwhite female tenants to trespass and conduct business do not raise an inference of discrimination, and his comparator evidence regarding lease renewal offers is insufficient because he did not allege he or Walt sought the superior apartment or were offered less favorable terms than similarly situated persons of a different sex. 12(b)(6) Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege [CLAIM] based on [CLASS]. His allegations lack adequate comparator evidence showing he and Walt were treated differently from similarly situated nonwhite persons. The comparison between Walt's lease renewal offer and advertised rent for Apartment 4F does not establish [CLASS] discrimination without showing Walt sought that apartment or was offered worse terms than nonwhite comparators. 12(b)(6) Age is not a protected characteristic under the FHA, so plaintiff cannot state a claim for age discrimination under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a) or (b). 12(b)(6) Plaintiff lacks statutory standing to sue under § 1692g because he is not a consumer under the FDCPA (not obligated or allegedly obligated to pay the debt). He also fails to state a claim under § 1692d because he alleges no conduct with the natural consequence of harassing, oppressing, or abusing any person in connection with debt collection. He lacks statutory standing under § 1692e(2) and (5) because the debt collection activity was not directed at him and he alleges no injurious exposure beyond reading a letter addressed to Walt. row_id: DT-PURE|10164858_2021_Miller v. Coastline Management_alsd
case_name: Miller v. Coastline Management
masked_text: Plaintiff's FHA claims fail because she cited 42 U.S.C. § 3601 (which merely states the FHA's general purpose) and § 3605 (which applies to real estate transactions like selling, brokering, or appraising), neither of which provides a cause of action for discrimination experienced while living in a condo unit. Pro se plaintiff Fredrika Miller sued Coastline Management and Beachcomber Homeowner Association alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on discrimination she and her mother experienced while living in their condo unit, citing her CPTSD and her mother's walker use as bases for discrimination. The court dismissed the FHA claims with prejudice, finding Miller failed to state a plausible cause of action under the cited statutory provisions (42 U.S.C. § 3601, which establishes only general FHA purpose, and § 3605, which applies to real estate transactions, not tenancy-related discrimination claims). Plaintiff cited § 3601 (statement of FHA policy, not a cause of action) and § 3605 (which applies only to real estate transactions, not housing discrimination during occupancy). Plaintiff alleged discrimination based on sex, [CLASS] (CPTSD and elderly mother with walker), and national origin (American Indian heritage) but failed to allege facts plausibly supporting a claim under the cited FHA provisions. Court applied Iqbal/Twombly pleading standard and found plaintiff failed to state a plausible FHA claim. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) — failure to state a claim Criminal statutes cited do not create private causes of action for civil enforcement. Federal criminal statutes require express Congressional intent to create a private right of action, which is absent here. Alabama law does not automatically create civil causes of action for criminal violations absent a breach of duty owed to plaintiff. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) — failure to state a claim

row_id: DT-PURE|10195167_2024_Goldstein v. The Bowery_nysd

masked_text: Plaintiff's FHA claims against Bowery Mission defendants were dismissed because his allegations do not support an inference of discriminatory motivation based on his Jewish religion, and district courts have concluded the FHA does not apply to shelters. masked_text: Plaintiffs' FHA claim fails because they have not explained how homeowners insurance claim adjustments fall within the scope of 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a)-(f), and their vague, conclusory allegations of discriminatory motive are insufficient to state a plausible claim; dismissal is also warranted under Rule 41(b) due to plaintiffs' history of dilatoriness and failure to comply with court orders. masked_text: The court granted defendant HOA's motion for judgment on the pleadings and dismissed all claims, holding that the FHA does not protect against discrimination based on political expression, the ADA does not apply to private residential facilities, the First Amendment claim was collaterally estopped by prior state-court rulings, and the HOA did not breach its CCRs when it enforced its sign restrictions and temporarily suspended community facility access. The court also denied plaintiffs' motions to remand and to recuse the presiding judge. The court dismissed the FHA claim because plaintiffs failed to state a plausible claim under the FHA, which protects against discrimination based on [CLASS], color, religion, sex, [CLASS], or national origin—not political expression or [CLASS]-based pool access. The court did not reach the merits of whether the [CLAIM] was reasonable. Rule 12(c) - Judgment on the Pleadings The ADA claim was dismissed because the private residential pool is not a public [CLAIM] covered by the ADA. The breach of contract claim was dismissed because plaintiffs' own allegations established that Murphy violated the CCRs by displaying signs exceeding the one-square-foot limit, and the BHOA properly enforced the covenant through discretionary suspension of facility access, which constituted no breach by the BHOA. Rule 12(c) - Judgment on the Pleadings

case_name: Lee v. Omaha Housing Authority Foundation Inc.
masked_text: Plaintiff failed to state plausible FHA claims because he made no allegations regarding his own protected characteristics and failed to allege facts showing a causal connection between any protected activity and the OHA's adverse actions, as his allegations about [CLAIM] were vague and conclusory. Hasani Lee, proceeding pro se and in forma pauperis, sued the Omaha Housing Authority alleging it violated the Fair Housing Act by making false police reports and filing a false eviction action against him after he was acting as power of attorney for his [CLASS] father. The court dismissed Lee's FHA claims at initial review, finding he failed to plead facts establishing a retaliation claim because his allegations were vague, failed to specify what [CLAIM] was being sought, and failed to allege a causal connection between any protected activity and the adverse actions. Plaintiff failed to allege plausible facts regarding what [CLAIM] was being sought, whether it was requested from the OHA, or any causal connection between the [CLAIM] request and the adverse action (false police reports and eviction filing). Allegations were too vague to state a plausible claim. Failure to state a claim (§ 1915(e)(2)(B)) Plaintiff failed to allege any facts regarding [CLASS], color, religion, sex, [CLASS], national origin, or [CLASS] as the basis for the OHA's actions, which are required elements of an FHA discrimination claim. Failure to state a claim (§ 1915(e)(2)(B)) Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing he engaged in protected activity under the FHA or that any protected conduct was the reason for the OHA's false statements and eviction action. The complaint lacks any causal connection between the alleged [CLAIM] request and the adverse actions taken. Failure to state a claim (§ 1915(e)(2)(B)) § 1983 constitutional claims failed because plaintiff did not allege a liberty interest in remaining on the property and thus no deprivation of constitutional rights. 18 U.S.C. § 1001 provides no private right of action. Nebraska criminal statutes (§§ 28-613, 28-907) provide no civil remedy. § 30-2473 applies only to estate administration. State tort claims are barred by the Nebraska Political Subdivisions Tort Claims Act (PSTCA) intentional-torts exception and pre-suit notice requirements. Failure to state a claim (§ 1915(e)(2)(B)); no private right of action; PSTCA bar

row_id: DT-PURE|10350993_2025_Deitch v. Medstar Medical Group Southern Maryland LLC_mdd
source_file: 10350993_2025_Deitch v. Medstar Medical Group Southern Maryland LLC_mdd
case_name: Ronald S. Deitch v. Medstar Medical Group, Southern Maryland LLC
masked_text: Plaintiff failed to state an FHA discrimination claim because his own allegations negated any plausible inference that the defendants' adverse actions (false police report and eviction) were taken because of his [CLASS], as he alleged the motive was retaliation for his advocacy unrelated to [CLASS]. Ronald Deitch, a [CLASS] tenant with multi system atrophy, sued Habitat America LLC (his landlord) and others alleging Fair Housing Act violations after Habitat's property managers allegedly made a false police report that led to his arrest and eviction. The court granted Habitat's motion to dismiss, finding Deitch failed to state an FHA claim because his own allegations showed the alleged retaliation was motivated by his advocacy for himself and neighbors, not by his [CLASS], and the claim was also time-barred. Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege a sufficient nexus of causation between his [CLASS] and the adverse action (false police report leading to eviction). Plaintiff's own allegations negate discrimination based on [CLASS], showing instead that the false report was made in retaliation for conduct unrelated to his [CLASS] (holding defendants to the lease and helping neighbors). Court found no plausible inference that the adverse action was taken 'because of' the [CLASS] as required under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(2)(A). 12(b)(6) IIED claim failed because making a false police report is not 'extreme and outrageous' under Maryland law and plaintiff did not allege severe emotional distress caused by Habitat defendants. § 1983 claim failed because Habitat defendants are not persons acting under color of state law. ADA Title III claim failed because residential apartment complexes do not constitute public accommodations under the ADA, and plaintiff did not allege discrimination because of [CLASS]. 12(b)(6)

row_id: DT-PURE|10361741_2025_Winston v. HON Partners II LLC_txed
case_name: Nadia Winston v. HON Partners II LLC et al.
masked_text: The court granted Defendant Mulvaney's motion to dismiss because the plaintiff's complaint and amended complaint failed to allege any cognizable claim against her specifically, as all alleged wrongful conduct was attributed to other parties (HON Partners, Dallas Housing Authority), and plaintiff had already been given an opportunity to amend. Pro se plaintiff Nadia Winston sued HON Partners II LLC and property manager Marissa Mulvaney in federal court alleging discrimination, retaliation, breach of lease, negligence, defamation, and Violence Against Women Act violations. The court granted Mulvaney's motion to dismiss with prejudice because the plaintiff's amended complaint failed to allege any actions taken by Mulvaney specifically, instead attributing all alleged misconduct to other parties, and plaintiff had already been afforded an opportunity to amend her complaint. Plaintiff failed to allege a plausible theory of recovery under any statute (FHA, ADA, Fourteenth Amendment) and failed to connect any discriminatory conduct to Defendant Mulvaney, who is not mentioned in the pleadings. The court found Plaintiff did not provide fair notice of the claims against this defendant. 12(b)(6) Plaintiff made conclusory statements of retaliation without legal basis or factual support and failed to allege any actions by Defendant Mulvaney. The court found Plaintiff did not carry her burden to plausibly allege entitlement to relief. 12(b)(6) All non-FHA claims were dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim. Plaintiff failed to allege any conduct by Defendant Mulvaney in connection with any of these causes of action. For defamation, Plaintiff did not allege the required elements. For contract breach, Plaintiff admitted Defendant Mulvaney was not a party to the lease. For negligence, Plaintiff failed to connect the mold inspection findings to Defendant Mulvaney. For VAWA, Plaintiff alleged only HON Partners' conduct. For fraud, Plaintiff failed to plead with particularity under Rule 9(b) and did not allege Defendant Mulvaney's involvement. 12(b)(6)

row_id: DT-PURE|10368942_2025_Baez v. New York State Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance_nysd
source_file: 10368942_2025_Baez v. New York State Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance_nysd
case_name: Baez v. New York State Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance
masked_text: The court dismissed all claims against the state and city defendants on procedural grounds, including lack of Article III standing (individual plaintiffs received ERAP benefits or never applied, and the organizational plaintiff lacked sufficient connection to its mission), sovereign immunity for OTDA, qualified immunity for the OTDA commissioner, and the FHA claims were time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations. [CLASS] and [CLASS] NYCHA public housing residents and Residents to Preserve Public Housing sued OTDA, NYCHA, and its commissioner alleging [CLASS] and [CLASS] discrimination in the state's ERAP program, which allegedly deprioritized public housing tenants, and NYCHA's failure to recertify incomes during the pandemic. The court granted all motions to dismiss on standing, sovereign immunity, qualified immunity, and statute of limitations grounds without reaching the merits of the discrimination claims. Individual plaintiffs Baez and Gil-Frederick lack standing because they received maximum ERAP benefits and cannot suffer future harm; Johnson lacks standing because she never applied for ERAP and failed to allege she was prevented from applying on equal footing. RPPH lacks associational standing because the connection between income recertification and its core mission of preserving public housing is tenuous, and diversion of resources does not constitute concrete injury. 12(b)(1) Same standing deficiencies as [CLAIM] claim; individual plaintiffs lack Article III standing and RPPH lacks associational standing. 12(b)(1) FHA claims are time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations. Plaintiffs were on notice of alleged discrimination in 2020-2021 but did not file suit until April 2024. The continuing violation doctrine does not apply because plaintiffs were aware of the alleged discrimination and failed to act timely, and the focus is on the time of the discriminatory act, not when consequences became painful. 12(b)(1) Non-FHA claims dismissed on same standing grounds as FHA claims; individual plaintiffs lack Article III standing and RPPH lacks associational standing. 12(b)(1)

row_id: DT-PURE|10378598_2025_West v. Landau_mied
case_name: Darryl West v. Marc Landau and Drinda Osborne
masked_text: The FHA claim was properly dismissed because West failed to allege that his [CLASS] was the basis for the alleged eviction—his claim was based on alleged retaliation for reporting criminal conduct to police and cooperating with law enforcement, not [CLASS] discrimination. Darryl West, proceeding pro se, sued his landlord Drinda Osborne and her attorney Marc Landau alleging Fair Housing Act, ADA, and state law violations arising from an alleged lifetime housing agreement and attempted eviction. The court summarily dismissed the complaint, finding that West failed to state a plausible FHA claim because his eviction challenge was based on alleged retaliation for cooperating with law enforcement, not on [CLASS] discrimination. The court dismissed the FHA claim because West failed to plausibly allege that his [CLASS] was the basis for the defendants' alleged misconduct. The basis for West's suit was retaliation for reporting theft and cooperating with law enforcement, not discrimination based on [CLASS], and thus did not constitute discrimination prohibited by the FHA. Dismissed under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) The ADA claim failed because private residential housing is not covered by the ADA and defendants are private citizens not subject to the statute. The § 1983 retaliation claim failed because defendants are private citizens and West failed to plausibly allege they acted under color of state law. The civil conspiracy claim failed because it depends on an adequately pled constitutional violation. Criminal claims (witness tampering and obstruction of justice) failed because private citizens lack authority to bring criminal charges and criminal statutes do not confer a private cause of action. State law claims were dismissed under supplemental jurisdiction doctrine after all federal claims were dismissed. Dismissed under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) and 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3)

row_id: DT-PURE|10380212_2025_Fontaine v. CGI_nyed
case_name: Fontaine v. CGI
masked_text: Plaintiff's FHA claim fails because she has not alleged any facts to support FHA liability—she has not stated what [CLASS] she lives with or explained what reason she was given for the alleged denial of an upgrade to her apartment, making the conclusory allegations of discrimination insufficient to state a plausible claim. Pro se plaintiff Matiya Fontaine, a [CLASS] [CLASS] woman residing in Brooklyn, sued CGI, Lineage Properties, Empire State Management Co., La Cabana Apartments, and individual defendants alleging Fair Housing Act violations, Section 1981, and Title VI claims based on being refused apartment renovations and an ADA upgrade to a larger unit, and being threatened with termination from her housing assistance program. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a plausible claim, finding the allegations too conclusory to support an inference of discrimination based on [CLASS] or [CLASS], and granted plaintiff thirty days leave to amend. Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to state a plausible FHA claim. She did not specify what [CLASS] or condition she lives with, nor did she explain the reason given for denial of the upgrade. Conclusory allegations without factual support are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly. 12(b)(6) Plaintiff's allegations consist only of conclusory statements that she is a [CLASS] woman who was denied a renovation request. The court cannot infer discrimination merely from [CLASS] identity and denial of a request without factual allegations explaining the reason for denial or circumstances giving rise to an inference of discrimination. 12(b)(6) Plaintiff failed to allege facts supporting an inference that she was subjected to retaliatory conduct or that she exercised her FHA rights. The complaint lacks details necessary to plausibly allege retaliation under the FHA. 12(b)(6) Plaintiff's § 1981 and Title VI claims suffer from the same pleading deficiency as her FHA claims. She alleges only conclusory statements that she is a [CLASS], [CLASS] woman denied renovations and an upgrade, without factual allegations showing intentional discrimination or that discrimination was a substantial or motivating factor in defendants' actions. The standard for these statutes is more exacting than the FHA standard, which plaintiff failed to meet. 12(b)(6)

row_id: DT-PURE|10595244_2025_Askins v. Prestige Management Inc._nysd
case_name: Delroy Askins v. Prestige Management Inc.
masked_text: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims because he failed to allege facts showing he has a [CLASS] as defined by the FHA or that any adverse actions taken against him were motivated by his [CLASS]. Pro se plaintiff Delroy Askins sued Prestige Management Inc. and building superintendent Lowell Hendricks alleging [CLASS] discrimination under the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act based on being assaulted, having his medical supplies taken, and being denied access to the community room. The court dismissed all claims for failure to state a claim because plaintiff failed to allege facts establishing he has a [CLASS] as defined by the statutes or that any adverse actions were motivated by his [CLASS], though the court granted plaintiff 30 days' leave to amend. Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing he has a [CLASS] as defined by the FHA or that any adverse actions were motivated by his [CLASS]. The complaint does not plausibly allege discriminatory motivation at the pleading stage. 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) Section 1983 claims fail because defendants are private parties not acting under color of state law; ADA Title III does not apply to residential housing; ADA Title II and Rehabilitation Act claims fail because plaintiff alleges no facts describing the nature of his [CLASS] or connecting the adverse actions to [CLASS] discrimination. 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii)

row_id: DT-PURE|10598089_2025_(PS) Moore v. C.F.Y. Development Inc._caed
case_name: Charlesetta Moore, SR. v. C.F.Y. Development Inc., et al.
masked_text: The complaint was dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege membership in a protected class and failed to plead facts showing different treatment because of protected class status, as a single [CLASS] slur and generalized allegations of poor treatment are insufficient to state a [CLAIM] claim. Plaintiff Charlesetta Moore, proceeding pro se and in forma pauperis, sued C.F.Y. Development Inc. and individual defendants alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on discriminatory treatment at Galt Place Senior Apartments, including rent increases, service failures, and a [CLASS] slur. The court dismissed the first amended complaint for failure to state a claim because plaintiff failed to allege membership in a protected class and failed to plead facts showing she was treated differently because of protected class status. Plaintiff failed to allege she is a member of a protected class and failed to allege facts showing she received different treatment because of protected class status. A single [CLASS] slur, while deplorable, is insufficient to establish an FHA violation without allegations that the defendants' conduct was motivated by plaintiff's protected status. Failure to state a claim

row_id: DT-PURE|10602120_2025_Lepp v. Mallett_mied
case_name: Heidi Grossman Lepp v. Conrad Mallet, Jr.
masked_text: Plaintiff's FHA claims fail because she only conclusorily alleged discrimination on the basis of [CLASS] and religion without pleading facts showing defendants acted with discriminatory intent based on those protected classes. Heidi Grossman Lepp, associated with Sugarleaf Church, sued Detroit officials and private parties alleging defendants conducted raids, inspections, and parking restrictions that violated her constitutional and federal statutory rights. The court denied plaintiff's motion to amend the complaint as futile, finding her FHA claims under §§ 3604 and 3617 failed because she only conclusorily alleged discrimination without factual allegations showing discriminatory intent based on [CLASS] or religion. Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to support an inference that defendants discriminated against her on the basis of protected classes (religion and [CLASS]). Allegations were conclusory without factual support showing discriminatory intent or animus. 12(b)(6) Plaintiff failed to specify which FHA rights (§§ 3603-3606) she exercised and failed to allege facts showing defendants acted with discriminatory animus. Conclusory allegations without factual support are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly. 12(b)(6) All non-FHA federal claims failed under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards due to conclusory allegations, lack of factual support, failure to identify applicable law, and lack of state action (for § 1983 claims against private attorney Madden and private company Woodward). State law claims dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction after all federal claims found futile. 12(b)(6)

row_id: DT-PURE|10625570_2025_Smith v. Resipro, LLC_ilnd
case_name: Smith v. ResiPro, LLC
masked_text: The court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA claim (Count II) as time-barred under the two-year limitations period, finding no basis to apply the continuing violations doctrine to extend the deadline, and dismissed the ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims (Count III) on the same timeliness grounds. Ronetta Smith, individually and as guardian for two [CLASS] adults, sued ResiPro LLC and ResiCap LP alleging they performed deficient construction work on her home purchased through the CHA Choose to Own program in Chicago's south side, with claims including FHA discrimination, ADA, and state law torts. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act claims as time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations, finding no continuing violation exception applied, and dismissed most state law claims for factual insufficiency or failure to state a claim. Court dismissed FHA claim (Count II) as barred by the two-year statute of limitations under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a). Discriminatory practice occurred in 2017; plaintiff filed complaint in September 2024. Continuing violations doctrine did not apply because plaintiff alleged only isolated conduct with no facts showing discrimination extending into the limitations period. 12(b)(6) Court dismissed ADA and Section 504 claims (Count III) as barred by Illinois' two-year statute of limitations for personal injury actions. Discriminatory conduct occurred in 2017; complaint filed September 2024. Continuing violations doctrine did not apply for same reasons as FHA claim. 12(b)(6)

row_id: DT-PURE|10634116_2025_Carroway v. Cepco Management Services, LLC_nced
case_name: Carroway v. Cepco Management Services, LLC
masked_text: The court dismissed plaintiffs' claims with prejudice for failure to prosecute under Rule 41(b), finding that plaintiffs Carroway and Young demonstrated dilatory conduct including failing to comply with court orders, canceling depositions multiple times, and causing counsel's withdrawal, while plaintiffs Shepard failed to respond to the show cause order entirely. Four individual plaintiffs sued Cepco Management Services and Lantana Crossing HOA asserting Fair Housing Act, civil rights, and state law claims related to allegedly discriminatory HOA rule enforcement. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss for failure to prosecute, finding plaintiffs engaged in dilatory conduct including failing to comply with court orders, repeated cancellation of depositions, and causing counsel withdrawal, warranting dismissal with prejudice. Case dismissed for failure to prosecute and failure to comply with court orders under Rule 41(b), not on the merits of the FHA claim. The court applied the four-factor Davis test and found dismissal warranted due to plaintiffs' pattern of dilatory conduct, personal responsibility for delays, prejudice to defendants, and ineffectiveness of lesser sanctions. Rule 41(b) dismissal for failure to prosecute Case dismissed for failure to prosecute and failure to comply with court orders under Rule 41(b), not on the merits of the FHA retaliation claim. The court applied the four-factor Davis test and found dismissal warranted due to plaintiffs' pattern of dilatory conduct, personal responsibility for delays, prejudice to defendants, and ineffectiveness of lesser sanctions. Rule 41(b) dismissal for failure to prosecute Case dismissed for failure to prosecute and failure to comply with court orders under Rule 41(b), not on the merits of the non-FHA claims. The court applied the four-factor Davis test and found dismissal warranted due to plaintiffs' pattern of dilatory conduct, personal responsibility for delays, prejudice to defendants, and ineffectiveness of lesser sanctions. Rule 41(b) dismissal for failure to prosecute

row_id: DT-PURE|10634273_2025_Felicie v. Hill_nysd
case_name: Bobby Felicie v. Octavia Hill, Assistant Inspector General of DOI
masked_text: The court dismissed plaintiff's complaint because he failed to allege facts showing he is [CLASS], that any defendant discriminated against him based on [CLASS] in a housing matter, or that any defendant violated his constitutional rights Pro se plaintiff Bobby Felicie sued various government officials including Assistant Inspector General Octavia Hill, state court judges, and HRA officials alleging constitutional violations, [CLASS] discrimination, and violations of the ADA, FHA, HIPAA, Privacy Act, CFAA, and ECPA. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim because plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts showing he is [CLASS], that any defendant discriminated against him based on [CLASS] in a housing context, or that defendants violated his constitutional rights, granting 30 days leave to replead. The court dismissed the complaint as frivolous under § 1915(e)(2)(B) because Plaintiff failed to allege facts supporting claims under the FHA, ADA, § 1983, HIPAA, Privacy Act, CFAA, or ECPA. The court found that Plaintiff did not allege he is [CLASS] and that a defendant discriminated against him based on [CLASS] in a housing matter, nor did he allege any defendant violated his constitutional rights or rights under CFAA/ECPA. HIPAA provides no private right of action, and the Privacy Act applies only to federal agencies. 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii), (iii)

row_id: DT-PURE|10634768_2025_Thompson v. PennyMac Loan Services LLC_mad
case_name: Dawn Thompson v. Evolve Bank & Trust and PennyMac Loan Services, LLC
masked_text: The court granted both defendants' motions to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), dismissing PennyMac because it had no involvement in the mortgage origination and no actual foreclosure was initiated, and dismissing Evolve because origination-related claims were time-barred and remaining post-assignment claims failed to state a plausible claim. Pro se plaintiff Dawn Thompson sued original mortgagee Evolve Bank & Trust and successor mortgagee PennyMac Loan Services alleging discriminatory mortgage origination, FHA underwriting standard violations, ADA [CLASS] discrimination in loan modifications, CARES Act violations, and various state law claims arising from her 2015 residential mortgage on a Worcester, Massachusetts property. The court granted PennyMac's motion to dismiss because PennyMac was not involved in origination and no actual foreclosure proceedings were ever initiated (plaintiff sold the home voluntarily). The court granted Evolve's motion to dismiss because the origination claims were barred by the applicable statute of limitations (the complained-of conduct occurred more than seven years before suit was filed) and the remaining post-assignment claims failed because Evolve had no involvement after assigning the mortgage to PennyMac in January 2019. Against PennyMac: no allegation that PennyMac was involved in origination (occurred 2015, assignment 2019); claim time-barred under applicable statute of limitations. Against Evolve: origination claims time-barred as complained-of conduct occurred more than seven years before filing. 12(b)(6) Against both defendants: regulations apply only when mortgagee 'commences foreclosure or acquires title.' Plaintiff failed to allege either defendant actually initiated foreclosure proceedings; instead she sold the property voluntarily. Regulations' triggering event did not occur. 12(b)(6) ADA claim: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege she is a qualified individual with [CLASS] (only alleged 'filed for [CLASS]' after 2016 car accident) and failed to show nexus between any discriminatory acts and [CLASS]. NIED/IIED: No plausible allegation of negligence or extreme/outrageous conduct; defendants' actions were lawful and typical. Consumer protection: No unfair or deceptive practice alleged; conduct was lawful and typical. Unjust enrichment: Assignment document clearly conveyed interest in mortgage to assignee. CARES Act: No private right of action; complained-of action predated moratorium; no allegation of actual foreclosure initiation. 12(b)(6)

row_id: DT-PURE|10641808_2025_Kelly v. Max Federal Credit Union (MAG+)_almd
case_name: Gregory Kelly, et al. v. Max Federal Credit Union, et al.
masked_text: The complaint is a nonsensical, frivolous shotgun pleading that fails to state any cognizable claims and must be dismissed sua sponte without opportunity to amend because amendment would be futile. Pro se plaintiffs Gregory and Annette Kelly filed a seventy-two-page shotgun complaint against Max Federal Credit Union and individuals alleging [CLASS] and [CLASS] discrimination in the denial of a home loan application, wrongful garnishment of bank funds, and various constitutional and statutory violations. The magistrate judge recommends dismissal sua sponte because the complaint is nonsensical, frivolous, and devoid of meaningful factual allegations, making amendment futile. The complaint is a frivolous shotgun pleading that fails to provide adequate notice of claims or factual allegations supporting relief. The court found the 72-page complaint contains virtually no meaningful factual allegations, conclusory and vague assertions, and multiple claims against all defendants without specifying individual liability. Amendment is futile given the plaintiff's history of filing similar meritless shotgun pleadings. Shotgun pleading dismissal

row_id: DT-PURE|10672101_2025_Prendergast v. Wode Cooper Companies Atcheson Place Lofts_ohsd
source_file: 10672101_2025_Prendergast v. Wode Cooper Companies Atcheson Place Lofts_ohsd
case_name: Carla Prendergast v. Woda Cooper Companies Atcheson Place Lofts, et al.
masked_text: Source of income is not a protected characteristic under the Fair Housing Act, which prohibits discrimination only because of [CLASS], color, religion, sex, [CLASS], [CLASS], or national origin, so plaintiff fails to state an FHA claim. Carla Prendergast, proceeding pro se and in forma pauperis, sued her former and prospective landlords Woda Cooper Companies/Atcheson Place Lofts and Metropolitan Holdings/Triumph Apartments, along with the Legal Aid Society of Columbus and Ohio Adult Parole Authority, alleging Fair Housing Act violations, due process violations under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, and state law claims stemming from her loss of housing. The court dismissed all federal claims, including her FHA source-of-income discrimination claim, because source of income is not a protected characteristic under the FHA, and declined supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims. Source of income is not a protected characteristic under the FHA, which prohibits discrimination only on the basis of [CLASS], color, religion, sex, [CLASS], [CLASS], or national origin. Plaintiff failed to allege membership in a protected class and therefore failed to state a plausible FHA claim. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) The § 1983 claim fails because Woda Cooper Companies and Atcheson Place Lofts are private entities, not state actors, and filing an eviction proceeding is not state action. State law claims lack federal question or diversity jurisdiction and are dismissed without prejudice under supplemental jurisdiction doctrine. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii); 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3)

row_id: DT-PURE|10678137_2025_Ogando v. Napolitano_nyed
case_name: Luis E. Ogando v. John J. Napolitano, Esq.
masked_text: The court dismissed all claims by a pro se plaintiff arising from a 2006 home purchase and subsequent foreclosure and eviction because claims related to state court proceedings were barred by the Eleventh Amendment, Rooker-Feldman doctrine, and res judicata, and the remaining federal statutory claims under the FHA, ECOA, TILA, RESPA, and § 1983 failed on the merits because plaintiff never alleged discrimination on any protected characteristic, lacked standing as a non-borrower, and filed well outside applicable statutes of limitations. Pro se plaintiff Luis Ogando sued multiple defendants—including mortgage lenders, attorneys, a realtor, and the New York Supreme Court—arising from a 2006 home purchase in which he used a credit-worthy intermediary (Mateo) as the nominal borrower, was allegedly promised the deed would be transferred to him, and was ultimately evicted after Mateo entered a short sale. The court first dismissed claims related to state court proceedings under the Eleventh Amendment (as to the NY Supreme Court), Rooker-Feldman (as to the eviction judgment), and res judicata (as to the foreclosure). The court then dismissed all remaining federal claims—under the FHA, ECOA, TILA, RESPA, and § 1983—because plaintiff failed to allege discrimination based on any protected characteristic, was not a borrower under TILA or RESPA, the TILA limitations period had expired in 2007, and the named private parties were not state actors, before declining supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims. Plaintiff alleged FHA, RESPA, TILA, ECOA, and § 1983 claims but failed to allege discrimination based on any protected characteristic under FHA or ECOA; TILA claim is time-barred (one-year statute of limitations from August 2006 closing); RESPA claim lacks factual support; § 1983 claims fail because defendants are private actors not acting under color of state law. Court dismissed under § 1915(e)(2)(B) as frivolous and failing to state a claim. 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)

row_id: DT-PURE|10705497_2025_Abraham Shitrai Israel and Sarah Iris Israel v. Barbara Guinn, et al._nynd
source_file: 10705497_2025_Abraham Shitrai Israel and Sarah Iris Israel v. Barbara Guinn, et al._nynd
case_name: Abraham Shitrai Israel and Sarah Iris Israel v. Barbara Guinn, et al.
masked_text: The court dismissed Plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act claim without prejudice for failure to state a claim, finding the complaint was devoid of allegations of discrimination based on a protected characteristic; the court also dismissed the Eighth Amendment claim with prejudice and gave Plaintiffs leave to amend the complaint within thirty days. Plaintiffs Abraham Shitrai Israel and Sarah Iris Israel, a pro se [CLASS] married couple, sued state and county officials including the New York State Office of Temporary [CLASS] Assistance and Onondaga County DSS workers, alleging violations of constitutional rights and the Fair Housing Act after being denied emergency public assistance for housing repairs and temporary shelter. The court adopted in part and rejected in part the Magistrate Judge's Report-Recommendation, dismissing the FHA claim without prejudice for failure to allege discrimination based on a protected characteristic, dismissing the Eighth Amendment claim with prejudice, and granting Plaintiffs leave to amend the complaint within thirty days. The complaint was devoid of any allegations of discrimination based on [CLASS], color, religion, sex, [CLASS], or national origin as required under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a). While the FHA also prohibits discrimination based on [CLASS] under § 3604(f)(2), the complaint failed to allege facts plausibly connecting the denial of benefits to [CLASS] discrimination. Dismissal without prejudice Procedural due process claims were subject to dismissal because plaintiffs failed to exhaust available Article 78 remedies under New York law, which provide an adequate post-deprivation remedy for random, unauthorized acts by state employees. Eighth Amendment claims were dismissed with prejudice because the Eighth Amendment protects only individuals convicted of crimes. § 1983 claims seeking relief for FHA violations were dismissed because the FHA contains a comprehensive enforcement mechanism that precludes § 1983 relief for FHA-based claims. Dismissal without prejudice (except Eighth Amendment dismissed with prejudice)

row_id: DT-PURE|10708675_2025_J. F. and on behalf of her adolescents and mother v. LUIS VENTURA_txnd
source_file: 10708675_2025_J. F. and on behalf of her adolescents and mother v. LUIS VENTURA_txnd
case_name: J. F. and on behalf of her adolescents and mother v. LUIS VENTURA
masked_text: The magistrate judge recommended dismissal without prejudice of all claims on three independent grounds: (1) lack of subject matter jurisdiction over claims J.F. brought on behalf of her mother and [CLASS] because a non-lawyer cannot represent others in federal court; (2) insufficient service of process for all claims; and (3) failure to state a claim under the ADA or FHA as to J.F.'s own claims because she pleaded insufficient facts to support either discriminatory intent or [CLAIM]. Pro se plaintiff J.F. sued her landlord Luis Ventura asserting violations of the ADA, FHA, and Texas Property Code, alleging discriminatory practices including threats of eviction affecting herself, her mother, and her adolescent [CLASS]. The magistrate judge recommended dismissal without prejudice on three separate grounds: J.F. lacked standing to represent her mother and [CLASS] as a non-attorney under 28 U.S.C. § 1654; she failed to timely effectuate service of process even after receiving multiple court-granted extensions; and as to her own claims she failed to plead sufficient facts to show discriminatory intent, [CLAIM], or any other cognizable basis under the ADA or FHA to prevent eviction. Plaintiff failed to plead facts showing that defendant's eviction action had a [CLAIM] on her as a person with a [CLASS] compared to persons without a [CLASS], nor did she allege discriminatory intent. The FHA does not provide a basis to prevent eviction absent such factual allegations. 12(b)(6) ADA Title III does not apply to private landlord-tenant eviction; plaintiff failed to allege defendant operated a public [CLAIM] or discriminated based on [CLASS]. Texas Property Code § 91.004(b) claim lacks factual support and stretches the statute beyond its natural reading; plaintiff pleaded no facts of discriminatory behavior or recognized cause of action. 12(b)(6)

row_id: DT-PURE|10731728_2025_Irish Horton v. Beacon Woods East Master Association, Inc., Ronnie Armstrong, and Christopher Skene_flmd

case_name: Irish Horton v. Beacon Woods East Master Association, Inc., Ronnie Armstrong, and Christopher Skene

case_name: Stephen Gray, et al. v. Warren Verbanec, et al.
masked_text: The court dismissed the complaint with prejudice because pro se plaintiffs failed to allege facts showing that defendant Warren Verbanec, a private HOA member, acted under color of state law as required for a §1983 claim, and the complaint lacked any specific factual allegations supporting the conclusory claims of conspiracy and discrimination. Pro se plaintiffs Stephen and Mikyong Gray filed suit against Warren Verbanec and others, alleging an eleven-year conspiracy to deprive Ms. Gray of civil rights through harassment and discrimination based on [CLASS], color, sex, national origin, and age, invoking 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982, 1983, 1985(3), and 3601–3619 (Fair Housing Act). The court construed the complaint as a single §1983 claim on behalf of Ms. Gray only. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss with prejudice, finding that the complaint failed to allege facts showing Verbanec acted under color of state law—since the Sunset Ridge Road Association is a private HOA and not a governmental entity—and that the complaint was entirely devoid of specific factual allegations to support its conclusory claims of conspiracy and discrimination. Plaintiffs failed to allege sufficient facts to state a claim under § 1983 because they did not plausibly allege that defendant acted under color of state law. A private HOA is not a governmental entity or functional equivalent thereof, and the complaint contains no factual allegations supporting an inference of state action. Additionally, the complaint is devoid of any plausible, specific factual allegations to support conclusory claims of conspiracy and discrimination. 12(b)(6)

row_id: DT-PURE|3200963_2016_Dorothy Hartman v. Bank of New York Mellon_ca3
source_file: 3200963_2016_Dorothy Hartman v. Bank of New York Mellon_ca3
case_name: Dorothy Hartman v. Bank of New York Mellon
masked_text: The Third Circuit affirmed dismissal because Hartman's complaint failed to adequately plead discriminatory purpose—she alleged defendants denied refinancing based on information from the City about utility nonpayment and property valuation, not based on her protected status. [CLASS] discrimination claims under the 14th Amendment failed because plaintiff did not allege execution of a government policy or custom. [CLASS] discrimination claims were conclusory. row_id: DT-PURE|4016914_2016_Thomas Wilson v. Warren County, Illinois_ca7
case_name: Thomas Wilson and Randy Brown v. Warren County, Illinois, Martin Edwards, Thomas Carithers, Albert Algren, Ronald Hanson, Mark Johnson, and Douglas Reiners
masked_text: The Seventh Circuit affirmed dismissal of Wilson's FHA claim because the complaint failed to allege facts plausibly showing the private defendants acted because of his [CLASS], as their conduct appeared motivated by a business dispute rather than Wilson's psychological conditions. Wilson's FHA claim under § 3617 and § 3604(f)(1) alleging that private defendants intentionally triggered his [CLASS] to prevent him from objecting to property removal failed to plausibly allege that defendants acted because of his [CLASS]. The complaint alleged business disputes and property disagreements, suggesting defendants were motivated by those factors rather than [CLASS], and did not raise a plausible inference that defendants would not have removed the property absent the [CLASS]. 12(b)(6) Summary judgment was granted on § 1983 claims against both private and public defendants. Private defendants could not be held liable under color of state law because plaintiffs failed to present evidence of a meeting of minds or concerted effort with public defendants; Johnson's misrepresentation to state actors constitutes unilateral action insufficient for private actor liability. Public defendants were not personally responsible because evidence did not support that they knew the removal was unlawful or acted with deliberate indifference; their conduct was merely negligent. State-created danger claim failed because Algren's statement about needing a court order did not shock the conscience. Rule 56

row_id: DT-PURE|4450591_2017_Morgan v. Carrington Mortgage Services_ca10
case_name: Virginia Morgan v. Carrington Mortgage Services; Bank of America, N.A.
masked_text: The Tenth Circuit affirmed dismissal of Morgan's FHA claim because even assuming Bank of America notified Carrington of the HUD complaint, it was implausible that Carrington declined to review her loss-mitigation application because of her [CLASS] or protected activity, given that the loan had been foreclosed eighteen months earlier, the property had already been sold, and the foreclosure judgment had been affirmed on appeal. Virginia Morgan appealed from the dismissal of her claims that Carrington Mortgage Services and Bank of America violated the FHA, RESPA, and FDCPA after foreclosing on her home. Morgan alleged the defendants discriminated and retaliated against her by failing to review her post-foreclosure loss-mitigation application after HUD notified them of her [CLASS] discrimination complaint. The Tenth Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that Morgan failed to plausibly allege causation because by the time she submitted the March 2015 application, the loan had been foreclosed for eighteen months, the property had been sold, and the foreclosure judgment had been affirmed on appeal. Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege causation between [CLASS] and adverse action. The loan had been foreclosed 18 months prior, the property sold 6 months prior, and the foreclosure judgment affirmed on appeal before the March 16, 2015 application was submitted, making it implausible that Carrington declined to review the application because of plaintiff's [CLASS] rather than because there was no longer a loan. Rule 12(b)(6) Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege causation between protected activity (HUD complaint filed April 15, 2015) and adverse action (failure to review March 16, 2015 application). The temporal sequence and post-foreclosure context make it implausible that the failure to review was retaliatory rather than based on the absence of an active loan. Rule 12(b)(6) RESPA claim failed because plaintiff alleged only conclusory damages without factual allegations of actual harm, and the March 16, 2015 application was submitted six months after the sheriff's sale, outside the 37-day window requiring servicer evaluation. FDCPA claims failed because none of the three alleged communications (June 1 letter, June 25 hearing, June 29 writ) conveyed information regarding a debt as required by the statute. Rule 12(b)(6)

masked_text: The court dismissed plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act and ADA claims for failure to state a claim because plaintiffs did not identify which FHA provisions were violated or how the ADA was implicated, and legal conclusions of discrimination without supporting facts are insufficient. masked_text: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claim because she failed to plausibly allege she belonged to a protected class (her unspecified physical [CLASS] was conclusory) and failed to allege facts suggesting discriminatory motivation for the denial. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding plaintiff failed to plausibly allege facts establishing she was a member of a protected class or that discriminatory motivation caused the denial of housing. Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege membership in a protected class under the FHA ([CLASS]) by providing only a bare statement of an unspecified physical [CLASS], and failed to allege facts supporting a plausible inference of discriminatory motivation beyond conclusory allegations that she was denied housing because of her [CLASS], age, and financial status. 12(b)(6)

row_id: DT-PURE|9848981_2023_Byng v. Kelly_nynd
case_name: Kevin V. Byng v. Bob Kelly
masked_text: On IFP initial review, the court recommends that plaintiff's First Amendment freedom of association claims against both defendants and his FHA [CLASS] discrimination claim against defendant Kelly survive and require a response, while recommending dismissal of his Eighth Amendment, substantive due process, § 1437d(l)(3), and [CLASS]-based ADA/RA/FHA claims. Kevin Byng, a sixty-two year old pro se plaintiff with multiple [CLASS], sued the Executive Director and security officer of the Utica Municipal Housing Authority under § 1983, the ADA, the Rehabilitation Act, and the FHA, alleging that defendants repeatedly threatened him with eviction, harassed him, and denied him overnight guest privileges because of his associations with [CLASS] women, while also failing to maintain building security. The court conducted an IFP initial review and found that plaintiff's First Amendment intimate association claims and FHA [CLASS] discrimination claim against defendant Kelly plausibly survived, while his [CLASS]-based discrimination claims failed for lack of factual allegations connecting the adverse actions to his [CLASS]. The court recommended dismissal with prejudice of the Eighth Amendment, § 1437d, and substantive due process claims, and dismissal without prejudice of the remaining ADA/RA/FHA [CLASS] claims and the FHA [CLASS] discrimination claim against defendant Connelly, with leave to amend. Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that defendants' actions were taken because of his [CLASS]. The complaint contains no facts showing defendants knew of or discriminated against plaintiff specifically because of his [CLASS]. Dismissed without prejudice Plaintiff plausibly alleged that defendant Kelly threatened eviction, harassed plaintiff, and denied overnight guest privileges because of plaintiff's association with [CLASS] women, which could constitute discrimination in terms, conditions, or privileges of rental. Claim against Connelly dismissed without prejudice because plaintiff failed to allege Connelly's participation in the [CLASS] discrimination. Survives initial review as to defendant Kelly; dismissed without prejudice as to defendant Connelly Court analyzed plaintiff's allegations of threats, harassment, and intimidation by defendant Kelly under the § 3617 hostile housing environment standard, finding plaintiff plausibly alleged harassment sufficiently pervasive and severe because of membership in a protected class (association with African Americans) and imputable to defendant Kelly. Subsumed within [CLAIM] claim; analyzed under § 3604(b) hostile housing environment framework First Amendment intimate association claim survives because plaintiff plausibly alleged defendants violated his right to have overnight guests and subjected guests to harassment. § 1437d(l)(3) claim fails because the statute does not create an enforceable right to safe housing under § 1983. Substantive due process claim fails because alleged conduct (threats of eviction and broken lobby lock) does not shock the conscience and plaintiff has no special relationship with UMHA creating a duty to protect. ADA/RA claims fail at pleading stage because plaintiff did not allege defendants knew of or discriminated because of [CLASS]. First Amendment claim survives; § 1437d(l)(3) claim dismissed with prejudice; Fourteenth Amendment claims dismissed with prejudice; ADA/RA claims dismissed without prejudice

masked_text: The court dismissed the FHA claim because plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting any defendant discriminated against her on the basis of [CLASS], rather than merely finding that she was entitled to [CLAIM] under § 3604(f)(3)(B). Pro se plaintiff Rhonda L. Harris sued the Yonkers Department of Social Services, OTDA, and OAH alleging she and her four [CLASS] (identified as [CLASS]) were illegally evicted and denied housing and public benefits, seeking emergency shelter and housing accommodations. row_id: DT-PURE|9855309_2020_Stone v. 23rd Chelsea Associates, LLC_nysd
case_name: Stone v. 23rd Chelsea Associates, LLC
masked_text: Plaintiff's Fair Housing Act and related discrimination claims were dismissed as time-barred and for failing to allege sufficient facts to raise an inference of discriminatory intent based on [CLASS]; the vague allegations of discriminatory conduct did not plausibly connect any adverse treatment to plaintiff's protected class status. Richard E. Stone, an [CLASS] Section 8 voucher holder and [CLASS] veteran, sued his landlord and property management company alleging they charged him higher rent than similarly situated [CLASS] tenants, sided with [CLASS] tenants in disputes, monitored him, and made discriminatory comments. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding Stone's claims were time-barred and that his vague, conclusory allegations failed to raise a plausible inference of [CLASS] discrimination. Plaintiff failed to allege facts raising a plausible inference of discriminatory animus based on [CLASS]. Allegations that defendants charged higher rent, sided with [CLASS] tenants, and made discriminatory statements were conclusory and devoid of factual content (e.g., no information on similarly situated comparators, timing of incidents, or causal connection to protected class). 12(b)(6) FHA claim is time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations (42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(a)). The only conduct alleged within the limitations period (December 16, 2016 threat and March 17, 2017 eviction attempt) fails to raise an inference of discriminatory animus. The continuing violation doctrine does not apply because no unlawful act occurred during the limitations period. 12(b)(6) Title VI, § 1982, NYSHRL, and NYCHRL claims are analyzed under the same McDonnell Douglas framework as FHA claims and fail for the same reasons: conclusory allegations lacking factual specificity and failing to raise an inference of intentional discrimination. Federal Tort Claims Act claim is frivolous because it applies only to the United States, not private entities. 12(b)(6)

row_id: DT-PURE|9856749_2020_Ash v. City of N.Y._nysd
case_name: Ash v. City of New York
masked_text: The court granted judgment on the pleadings for defendants because the FHA claim was time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations, and the § 1983 claims failed because plaintiff did not adequately allege defendants acted under color of state law. Damon Ash, an [CLASS] Jewish man proceeding pro se, sued his former landlords Betty Jacobson and Laura Porschar (employees of the United Jewish Council) for housing discrimination based on [CLASS] and religion and related constitutional torts. The court granted defendants' motion for judgment on the pleadings, dismissing the FHA claim as time-barred by the two-year statute of limitations and dismissing the § 1983 claims for failure to adequately allege state action, while declining supplemental jurisdiction over state law defamation claims. The FHA claim is time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations. Plaintiff alleged discrimination through July 2016, but did not name defendants until December 21, 2018, well after the limitations period expired. The continuing violation doctrine does not apply, and relation back under Rule 15(c) is unavailable because defendants lacked notice of this particular action. Rule 12(c) — Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings Section 1983 claims dismissed because plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that defendants acted under color of state law; defendants were private employees of the United Jewish Council with no alleged state affiliation. No plausible conspiracy with state actors was alleged. State-law defamation claims dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction after all federal claims were dismissed. Rule 12(c) — Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings

masked_text: Plaintiff's FHA claims were properly dismissed because the complaint alleged only negligent care and inadequate supervision, not intentional discrimination or discriminatory animus against the [CLASS]; plaintiff failed to plead facts showing defendants treated Zlotnick worse than other residents due to his [CLASS].
