row_id: DT-PURE|9899197_2023_Meadows v. Buffalo Police Department_nywd
case_name: Carolette Meadows v. Buffalo Police Department, et al.
masked_text: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claim because she failed to allege a sufficient nexus between [CLASS] animus and any adverse housing action, noting that not every neighbor quarrel gives rise to a viable FHA claim. Plaintiff Carolette Meadows, proceeding pro se, sued her neighbor Rachel Eckert, the Buffalo Police Department, Erie County prosecutors, and others alleging constitutional violations, ADA claims, and Fair Housing Act claims stemming from a long-running neighborhood dispute involving property disputes and physical altercations. The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claim, finding she failed to allege a sufficient nexus between Eckert's [CLASS] statements and any adverse housing action, and also dismissed claims against government defendants for failure to state viable claims while granting plaintiff leave to amend. Court found no plausible nexus between alleged [CLASS] animus (social media posts) and any adverse housing action. Plaintiff failed to allege how Eckert's conduct was connected to plaintiff's exercise of fair housing rights; the dispute was characterized as a neighbor quarrel lacking the required nexus to an FHA-protected activity. 12(b)(6) Section 1981 claim dismissed for failure to allege causal link between [CLASS] and deprivation of protected right; § 1983 claims dismissed because defendant Eckert is not a state actor (merely calling police does not constitute state action); §§ 1985-1986 claims dismissed for failure to allege conspiracy; ADA claim dismissed because private violence does not give rise to ADA liability; § 1982 claim dismissed for failure to allege nexus between [CLASS] animus and interference with property rights. 12(b)(6)

row_id: DT-PURE|9900376_2024_Meadows v. Buffalo Police Department_nywd
case_name: Meadows v. Buffalo Police Department
masked_text: The court dismissed all FHA and civil rights claims against neighbor Eckert and the Erie County defendants, finding Eckert was not a state actor under § 1983, that Meadows failed to plead a sufficient nexus between [CLASS] animus and an adverse housing action under FHA § 3617, and that Erie County prosecutors' charging decisions were immune from Monell liability. Pro se plaintiff Carolette Meadows brought claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981–1983, 1985–1986, the ADA, and the FHA against her neighbor Rachel Eckert, the Buffalo Police Department, Erie County, and Erie County prosecutors, arising from a years-long neighbor feud in which Eckert allegedly harassed, physically assaulted, and racially targeted Meadows while police and prosecutors gave undue deference to Eckert's complaints. The court granted motions to dismiss filed by Eckert and the Erie County defendants, finding that Eckert was not a state actor, that Meadows failed to connect Eckert's [CLASS] animus to any adverse housing action as required for a viable FHA § 3617 claim, and that the Erie County prosecutors' charging decisions could not support a Monell claim. The action continues against the City of Buffalo and BPD defendants who answered the second amended complaint. Plaintiff failed to allege a nexus between [CLASS] animus and an adverse housing action. The court found that isolated acts of [CLASS] animus are insufficient; there must be a connection between a stray remark and the challenged action. Plaintiff's allegations of Eckert's [CLASS] statements were not connected to any factual allegations regarding interference with housing rights. 12(b)(6) Plaintiff failed to state viable claims under §§ 1981 and 1982 because she did not plausibly allege that Eckert deprived her of protected rights based on [CLASS]; claims under § 1983 failed because Eckert was not a state actor; § 1985 and 1986 claims failed due to conclusory conspiracy allegations without factual support; ADA claims failed because Eckert was not subject to any ADA title; Title VII claims failed because Eckert was not plaintiff's employer; state tort and conspiracy claims failed for lack of factual support. 12(b)(6)

case_name: Franklin v. The Jersey City Housing Authority
masked_text: HUD's Motion to Dismiss was granted because HUD enjoys sovereign immunity, the FHA does not provide a private right of action against HUD for failure to investigate, and Plaintiff lacks Article III standing against HUD. Pro se Plaintiff Edwina Franklin sued HUD and Jersey City Housing Authority alleging JCHA violated the FHA by denying her request to waive a recapture policy so she could sell her home and move to a one-story residence due to her [CLASS]-related [CLASS] limitations. The Court granted HUD's Motion to Dismiss, finding HUD immune from suit under sovereign immunity, that no private right of action exists against HUD under the FHA, and that Plaintiff lacks Article III standing against HUD; Plaintiff's claims against JCHA remain pending. Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under Article III standing doctrine. Plaintiff's alleged injury (JCHA's denial of recapture waiver) was not traceable to HUD, as 42 U.S.C. § 1437z-4(i) requires HUD to allow JCHA discretion in setting lending terms. Additionally, even if court ruled against HUD, it could not alter the mortgage terms set solely by JCHA, so injury would not be redressed by favorable judicial decision. 12(b)(1) and 12(b)(6) Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. FHA does not provide private right of action to sue HUD for failure to investigate FHA violations. ECOA waives sovereign immunity only for discrimination in provision of credit, but HUD did not lend plaintiff money. Procedural due process claim fails because alleged failure to investigate amounts to procedural violation, not concrete injury sufficient for Article III standing, and no cause of action exists for monetary damages from federal agencies. 12(b)(1) and 12(b)(6)

row_id: RD-PURE|10213380_2021_Payne v. City of San Antonio, Texas_txwd
source_file: 10213380_2021_Payne v. City of San Antonio, Texas_txwd
case_name: Payne v. City of San Antonio, Texas
masked_text: Plaintiffs failed to state a plausible FHA [CLASS] [CLAIM] claim because Mr. Payne did not allege facts showing his schizoaffective disorder substantially limits a major life activity, and his retaliation claim failed because Midcrown proffered a legitimate non-retaliatory reason (threatening Facebook post) for the eviction. Don Albert Payne and Gloria Jean Payne sued Midcrown Pavilion Apartments and SAHA employee Amy V. Carrillo alleging [CLASS] discrimination, failure to accommodate, and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act after being evicted following a request for covered parking near their apartment. The magistrate judge recommended granting defendants' motions to dismiss, finding plaintiffs failed to plausibly plead Mr. Payne's schizoaffective disorder substantially limited a major life activity to establish a qualifying [CLASS], and failed to rebut Midcrown's legitimate non-retaliatory reason for the eviction. Plaintiffs failed to plead a qualifying [CLASS] under the FHA by not alleging facts showing how Mr. Payne's schizoaffective disorder substantially limits a major life activity; they provided only a diagnosis without explaining the functional limitation. Additionally, plaintiffs failed to allege facts showing how denial of parking constitutes discrimination on account of [CLASS]. 12(b)(6) Plaintiffs failed to establish a prima facie retaliation claim under the FHA. Although temporal proximity existed between the [CLAIM] request (November 2017) and eviction (April 2018), Midcrown presented a legitimate, non-retaliatory reason for eviction—Mr. Payne's threatening Facebook post depicting weapons and threatening statements toward government officials. Plaintiffs alleged no facts suggesting pretext. Additionally, under Texas Property Code § 92.332(b)(2), eviction does not constitute retaliation where the tenant threatens personal safety. 12(b)(6) Section 1983 claims against Midcrown fail because Midcrown is a private entity and not a state actor; plaintiffs alleged only generalized allegations of cooperation with SAHA without facts establishing state attribution. Tort claims (IIED, negligence) fail because eviction pursuant to a lease contract does not rise to the level of extreme and outrageous conduct required. Breach of contract and covenant of quiet enjoyment claims were not permitted in the live pleading. Section 1986 and DTPA claims do not focus on Midcrown. 12(b)(6) Against Carrillo, plaintiffs failed to allege any act or omission by Carrillo personally regarding failure to accommodate. Plaintiffs alleged only that Carrillo sent correspondence attempting to mediate a disagreement, canceled an appointment, and requested more information—facts from which no factfinder could plausibly conclude Carrillo had Mr. Payne evicted in retaliation for requesting [CLAIM]. 12(b)(6) Against Carrillo, Section 1983 Fourth Amendment search and seizure claim fails because all allegations concern SAPD officers, not Carrillo. Section 1983 due process claim fails under qualified immunity because Carrillo presented exigent circumstances (threat of violence from Facebook post) justifying eviction without prior hearing, and plaintiffs failed to rebut this defense or cite clearly established law. Section 1985 conspiracy claim fails because it requires [CLASS] animus motivation, which plaintiffs did not allege. DTPA claim fails because Carrillo acted in official capacity as SAHA agent, and SAHA is not a 'person' under the DTPA; additionally, official immunity applies. 12(b)(6)

masked_text: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA [CLAIM] claim because he failed to allege any facts suggesting he has a [CLASS] within the meaning of the FHA and failed to allege facts regarding the nature of any specific [CLAIM] that defendants denied. Plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting he has a [CLASS] under the FHA and did not allege the nature of the [CLAIM] sought or that defendants discriminated in denying it. Court granted leave to amend to cure pleading defects. Dismissed with leave to amend Plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting he exercised rights under the FHA or that defendants coerced, intimidated, or threatened him in connection with exercise of FHA rights. Conclusory allegations and filing of a complaint against plaintiff do not constitute intimidation or retaliation under § 3617. Dismissed with leave to amend § 1983 claims dismissed because defendants are private parties not acting under color of state law; Title VII claims dismissed because plaintiff did not allege he was an employee; ADA Title III claims dismissed for failure to allege [CLASS] and specific [CLAIM] sought. Dismissed

case_name: Jerome Want v. Saundra Jones, Wayne Jones, City of Hagerstown, MD., Michael Sabol, Salvatore & Morton
masked_text: The court dismissed the complaint for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction because the plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to support his FHA or ADA claims, and diversity jurisdiction was unavailable as the parties were not citizens of different states. Pro se plaintiff Jerome Want sued his landlord, the City of Hagerstown, a city housing inspector, and a law firm over his deteriorating apartment, alleging violations of the FHA, ADA, and various state law claims. The court found Want's ADA claim failed because his landlord is not a public entity and his apartment is not a public [CLAIM], and his FHA claim failed because he alleged no discriminatory conduct in leasing and no refusal of a [CLAIM]. Lacking viable federal claims and unable to establish diversity jurisdiction because most parties were Maryland citizens, the complaint was dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. Court found plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to support an FHA claim. Plaintiff did not allege that landlord refused to make reasonable accommodations in rules or practices, nor that plaintiff was denied the opportunity to lease the apartment. The complaint's core allegations concern Maryland state law habitability violations, not FHA discrimination. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(i) ADA claims fail because landlord is not a public entity (Title II) and apartment is not a public [CLAIM] (Title III). Maryland state law claims fail for lack of diversity jurisdiction because only one defendant resides outside Maryland, and plaintiff cannot establish the requisite amount in controversy. Constitutional claims fail because landlord is not a state actor. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(i) and lack of subject matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332

row_id: RD-PURE|10644107_2025_Ballentine v. Bowery Residence Committee_nyed
case_name: Ballentine v. Bowery Residents' Committee
masked_text: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA and ADA claims because he failed to plead specific facts describing how he was punished and denied reasonable accommodations, or how those actions were due to his [CLASS]. Pro se plaintiff Quintin Ballentine sued Bowery Residents' Committee and government officials alleging violations of the Eighth Amendment, Fair Housing Act, ADA, and 18 U.S.C. § 242 based on conditions at a men's shelter in Brooklyn, claiming he was punished due to his [CLASS] ([CLASS] and anxiety) and denied reasonable accommodations. Plaintiff failed to plead specific facts describing how he was denied reasonable accommodations, by whom, or how those adverse actions were due to his [CLASS]. The complaint contains only conclusory allegations without factual content sufficient to state a plausible claim under the FHA. 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) Plaintiff alleged he was 'punished due to [his] [CLASS]' but failed to plead specific facts describing how he was punished, by whom, or how those adverse actions were due to his [CLASS], failing to meet the two-element test for FHA discrimination claims. 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) Eighth Amendment protections apply only to convicted prisoners and plaintiff alleged no conviction; 18 U.S.C. § 242 is a criminal statute that does not confer a private right of action; ADA Title III claim fails for lack of specific factual allegations regarding discrimination and denial of services due to [CLASS], and even if adequately pled, Title III provides only injunctive relief, not the monetary damages sought. 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii)

row_id: RD-PURE|10806943_2026_Gabriella Collette, for herself and on behalf of Channin Collette, an incapacitated person v. Utah State Developmental Center; Utah State Department of Human Services; State of Utah; Jarod Squire_utd
source_file: 10806943_2026_Gabriella Collette, for herself and on behalf of Channin Collette, an incapacitated person v. Utah State Developmental Center; Utah State Department of Human Services; State of Utah; Jarod Squire_utd
case_name: Gabriella Collette, for herself and on behalf of Channin Collette, an incapacitated person v. Utah State Developmental Center; Utah State Department of Human Services; State of Utah; Jarod Squire
masked_text: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claim (Count II) on Eleventh Amendment sovereign immunity grounds because Congress did not abrogate states' immunity when enacting the FHA, and Utah has not waived immunity under the circumstances. Gabriella Collette, as legal guardian of incapacitated Channin Collette with intellectual [CLASS] and [CLASS], sued Utah State Developmental Center, the Utah Department of Health and Human Services, the State of Utah, and employee Jarod Squire alleging, inter alia, an FHA violation for failure to protect Channin from sexual assault by a caregiver. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss the FHA claim on Eleventh Amendment sovereign immunity grounds, holding Congress did not abrogate state immunity in the FHA and Utah has not waived immunity where the injury arose from assault and battery. The FHA claim was dismissed on Eleventh Amendment immunity grounds. Congress did not abrogate States' Eleventh Amendment immunity in the FHA, and Utah has not waived immunity. The claim arises from assault and battery, which is specifically retained under Utah's Governmental Immunity Act. The court did not reach the merits of the FHA claim itself, dismissing on jurisdictional/immunity grounds rather than on the substantive elements of an FHA violation. 12(b)(6) All non-FHA claims (§ 1983, Title IX, ADA Title II, premise liability, negligence, gross negligence, sexual battery) were dismissed. § 1983 and premise liability claims were dismissed on Eleventh Amendment immunity grounds. Title IX and ADA Title II claims were dismissed for failure to plausibly allege the requisite elements (actual knowledge/deliberate indifference for Title IX; nexus to [CLASS] for ADA). Negligence, gross negligence, and sexual battery claims were dismissed on immunity grounds as vicarious liability claims against state defendants. 12(b)(6)

source_file: 10006353_2024_David Q. Webb v. Miami-Dade County Government_ca11
case_name: David Q. Webb v. Miami-Dade County Government
masked_text: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal, holding that the district court did not abuse its discretion in dismissing appellant's case because he failed to comply with the court's order to file a proper second amended complaint after being warned that failure to do so would result in dismissal. Pro se appellant David Webb sued Miami-Dade County Government, Miami-Dade County Homeless Trust, Camillus House (a non-profit supportive housing provider), and individual defendants, alleging Fair Housing Act and ADA violations related to his removal from a Camillus House residential facility for his angina [CLASS]. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal without prejudice, finding no abuse of discretion because Webb failed to file a proper second amended complaint after the court identified his pleading as a shotgun complaint and warned that failure to comply would result in dismissal. The district court dismissed the complaint under § 1915(e)(2)(B) screening as a shotgun pleading containing conclusory, vague, and immaterial facts not obviously connected to any particular cause of action. The court did not reach the substantive merits of the FHA [CLAIM] claim because the pleading failed to satisfy Rule 8 and Rule 10 notice requirements. Shotgun pleading / failure to comply with court order The district court dismissed all non-FHA claims under § 1915(e)(2)(B) screening as part of the shotgun pleading determination. The complaint failed to specify which defendants were responsible for which acts and asserted multiple claims against multiple defendants without adequate notice, preventing substantive analysis of the ADA, state law, and constitutional claims. Shotgun pleading / failure to comply with court order

row_id: RD-PURE|10636620_2025_Millerborg v. Blue Bonnet Trail, LLC_txnd
case_name: Casey Millerborg v. Blue Bonnet Trail LLC, et al.
masked_text: The court dismissed the case for lack of Article III standing because the plaintiff's complaint was conclusory and lacked sufficient factual detail about whether he personally experienced (as opposed to merely observed) the accessibility barriers at the property, failing to allege a concrete injury in fact. Casey Millerborg, a [CLASS] user, sued Blue Bonnet Trail LLC and its managers alleging that an apartment complex in Waxahachie, Texas violated the Fair Housing Act's [CLAIM] requirements due to accessibility barriers he observed during a visit. The court dismissed the case without prejudice for lack of Article III standing, finding Millerborg's complaint was conclusory and failed to allege sufficient facts showing he personally experienced the accessibility barriers rather than merely observing them, and failed to establish a likelihood of future injury for injunctive relief. Plaintiff lacked Article III standing because his complaint failed to allege with sufficient particularity that he personally experienced (rather than merely observed) any accessibility barriers, and he failed to establish a concrete future injury for purposes of seeking equitable relief. The court found the allegations conclusory and devoid of contextual details about when, where, and how plaintiff encountered the barriers. 12(b)(1)

source_file: 10672251_2025_Daniel Frishberg v. University of South Florida Board of Trustees_ca11
case_name: Daniel A. Frishberg v. University of South Florida Board of Trustees
masked_text: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed dismissal of FHA and state law claims based on Eleventh Amendment immunity but vacated and remanded to allow the plaintiff leave to amend to add Rehabilitation Act claims, which would not be barred by sovereign immunity. Daniel Frishberg, a University of South Florida student with a [CLASS], sued the university and building owner after his emotional support animal waiver was revoked when he repeatedly brought his cat into dorm common areas in violation of the [CLAIM] terms. The district court dismissed his Fair Housing Act and state law claims based on Eleventh Amendment immunity. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the dismissal of those claims but vacated and remanded, holding the district court erred by not giving the pro se plaintiff an opportunity to amend to add Rehabilitation Act claims, which are not barred by sovereign immunity when the state receives federal funding. District court dismissed on Eleventh Amendment immunity grounds, finding Congress had not abrogated sovereign immunity for Fair Housing Act claims against state entities. Appellate court affirmed the Eleventh Amendment analysis but vacated and remanded to allow plaintiff opportunity to amend complaint to add Rehabilitation Act claim, which would not be barred by Eleventh Amendment immunity because the university receives federal financial assistance. Eleventh Amendment immunity District court dismissed retaliation claim under Fair Housing Act on Eleventh Amendment immunity grounds. Appellate court affirmed the jurisdictional dismissal but remanded for opportunity to amend with Rehabilitation Act claim. Eleventh Amendment immunity District court dismissed ADA claim with prejudice for failure to state a claim (which plaintiff did not appeal). Fair Housing Act and Florida law claims dismissed on Eleventh Amendment immunity. Appellate court affirmed Eleventh Amendment dismissal but vacated to allow amendment adding Rehabilitation Act claim, which would not be barred by sovereign immunity because university receives federal financial assistance. Eleventh Amendment immunity (FHA and state law); ADA dismissed with prejudice for failure to state claim; Rehabilitation Act claim not yet addressed on merits

row_id: RD-PURE|10804889_2026_Perry v. Encore At Blvd One_ca10
case_name: Shannon Perry v. Encore At Boulevard One LLC
masked_text: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the dismissal of the Fair Housing Act claim, holding that the tenant's substantive challenges to the dismissal were waived for being raised only in the reply brief and lacked merit even if considered. Shannon Perry appealed the dismissal of her Fair Housing Act claim arising from an eviction dispute against Encore At Boulevard One LLC and individual defendants. The Tenth Circuit affirmed the dismissal, holding that Perry waived her substantive challenges by raising them only in a reply brief, and rejected her remaining procedural arguments regarding the TRO denial as moot, the ADA and Double Jeopardy claims, the timing of dismissal before discovery, and the denial of a guardian ad litem. The district court granted defendants' motion to dismiss the Fair Housing Act claim for failure to state a valid claim under the pleading standard. The appellate court affirmed, finding the tenant failed to adequately plead the FHA claim and noting that screening survival does not preclude later dismissal on a motion to dismiss. 12(b)(6) The district court summarily dismissed the ADA claim because an apartment residence is not a place of public [CLAIM], the Double Jeopardy Clause claim because it applies only to state actors and criminal proceedings (not civil evictions), and the § 1983 claim for the same reason. The appellate court affirmed, finding the tenant waived appellate challenge by failing to explain why the rulings were erroneous. 12(b)(6)

source_file: 9862537_2021_Mercer v. New York City Housing Authority_nysd
case_name: Robert Mercer v. New York City Housing Authority
masked_text: Plaintiff's mild intermittent asthma without complication does not substantially limit a major life activity to qualify as a cognizable [CLASS] under the FHA, and the complaint failed to allege that NYCHA knew or had reason to know of plaintiff's asthma. Pro se plaintiff Robert Mercer, a public housing tenant, sued NYCHA alleging failure to accommodate his asthma by not properly addressing mold in his apartment under the FHA's [CLAIM] provision. The court granted NYCHA's motion to dismiss, finding the complaint failed to adequately plead a cognizable [CLASS] (mild intermittent asthma does not substantially limit a major life activity) and failed to allege NYCHA knew of his condition. Plaintiff failed to adequately allege the first two elements of a [CLAIM] claim: (1) he did not allege a [CLASS] cognizable under the FHA because his diagnosis of 'mild intermittent asthma without complication' does not substantially limit a major life activity, and (2) he did not allege that defendant knew or reasonably should have known of his asthma condition. The court declined to invent factual allegations not pleaded in the complaint. 12(b)(6) A private citizen cannot bring a claim based solely on 24 C.F.R. § 5.703(f) because neither the United States Housing Act of 1937 nor the regulation itself creates an enforceable individual right of action; only HUD may enforce the regulation's requirements. 12(b)(6)

row_id: RD-PURE|9955146_2022_Jeffreys v. Carson_rid
case_name: Madeliene Y. Jeffreys v. Marcia L. Fudge, Secretary of U.S. Housing & Urban Development, et al.
masked_text: The court dismissed HUD from the case, declined to dismiss the Woonsocket Housing Authority and Ms. Ferri despite caption deficiencies, dismissed the Fair Housing Act claim for lack of private right of action, but allowed the § 1983 due process claim to proceed based on allegations that the WHA obstructed the live-in aide recertification process. Plaintiff Madeliene Jeffreys, who served as a live-in aide for her [CLASS] daughter and grandson in Section 8 housing, sued HUD, the Woonsocket Housing Authority, and a WHA employee after her recertification was denied when the WHA allegedly withheld a medical form and refused alternative documentation. The court granted HUD's motion to dismiss for failure to allege facts connecting HUD to the claimed wrongdoing, declined to dismiss the WHA and Ms. Ferri despite caption deficiencies, dismissed the FHA claim for lack of private right of action, but allowed the § 1983 procedural due process claim to proceed. The court held that Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968 (FHA) does not establish a private right of action for money damages, and therefore dismissed plaintiff's direct FHA claim. The court noted that while the FHA regulations require PHAs to approve live-in aides as reasonable accommodations, the FHA itself provides no private remedy. Dismissed for lack of private right of action under FHA The court held that plaintiff stated a plausible § 1983 due process claim by alleging that the WHA obstructed the recertification process by refusing to provide a duplicate form while insisting documentation be submitted on that withheld form, combined with allegations of false evidence and an arbitrary deadline. The court found a sufficient property interest in continued Section 8 assistance to warrant due process protection. Survives motion to dismiss; case proceeds against properly named defendants

case_name: Sarah Melton v. State of Oklahoma ex rel. University of Oklahoma
masked_text: The court dismissed the FHA [CLAIM] claim because plaintiff failed to plausibly allege a refusal to accommodate; the University began remediation efforts within days of the request, which did not constitute a refusal. Sarah Melton, a student at the University of Oklahoma, sued the University and individual officials alleging that her dormitory's toxic mold infestation caused her serious health problems and that the University violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing to accommodate her [CLASS] (heightened susceptibility to mold) through professional remediation. The court dismissed the FHA claim, finding that the University's prompt initiation of remediation efforts within days of the request did not constitute a refusal to accommodate. Court found that plaintiff failed to plausibly allege the element of refusal. The facts alleged demonstrated that remediation efforts began one day after the request and testing was agreed to shortly thereafter, which does not constitute a refusal to accommodate. Additionally, no allegations identified a refusal by any specific Individual Defendant. 12(b)(6) Fraud claims dismissed for failure to plead with particularity under Rule 9(b), lacking specific times, places, contents of false representations, and identification of which Individual Defendant made which statements. IIED claim dismissed as conduct alleged did not rise to level of 'extreme and outrageous' required under Oklahoma law. Private nuisance claim dismissed as allegations only supported public nuisance theory. Tortious interference with contract claim dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege that Individual Defendants acted in their own personal interests rather than the University's interests. 12(b)(6)

masked_text: The FHA [CLAIM] claim fails because the driveway apron was not within the property line of Rodriguez's residence but rather on an adjacent commercial lot, so it did not fall within the 'premises' of her dwelling that she is entitled to modify under § 3604(f)(3)(A). The court granted the City's motion to dismiss, holding that the FHA [CLAIM] claim failed because the driveway was not part of Rodriguez's premises but rather on an adjacent property, and the ADA claim failed because the driveway was not a City service. The court dismissed the FHA claim because the driveway apron was not part of the 'premises' of plaintiff's dwelling under the FHA—it was located on an adjacent property outside plaintiff's property line. The court held that while exterior accessible routes may be required, plaintiff sought to alter a public way outside a neighboring property, not to modify the premises she occupied. Plaintiff did not allege that aldermanic staff were aware of her [CLASS] or her June 2024 communications with CDOT regarding her need for the apron when they initiated action in February 2024, breaking the temporal nexus required for retaliation. 12(b)(6) The court dismissed the ADA Title II claim because the driveway apron was not a 'service, program, or activity' provided by the City—it was a privately permitted driveway created for a neighboring commercial property. Plaintiff did not allege that any actual City service (such as sidewalks or curb ramps) was inaccessible to her because of her [CLASS]. masked_text: The court denied Kris's motion to add [CLAIM] claims against the MHRA, finding that the four-month delay in processing her transfer request did not constitute an unreasonable delay or constructive denial where the delay was attributable to inadvertence and procedural issues rather than bad faith, and the request became moot upon her eviction. The court previously denied plaintiff's motion for summary judgment on FHA retaliation claims against the Dusseaults and Trust, and directed defendants to move for summary judgment on three of four remaining retaliation claims. The claims survive and proceed to trial. Motion for Summary Judgment Denied Plaintiff failed to plead facts showing the MHRA denied her [CLAIM] request before her eviction made it moot. The court found no evidence of unreasonable delay (four-month period from November 2017 to March 2018 was not unreasonable under totality of circumstances), no bad faith or willful intent to delay, and only inadvertence and bureaucratic mistakes, which do not constitute constructive denial of [CLAIM]. 12(b)(6) FHEO is a federal agency and § 1983 does not apply to federal actors; plaintiff failed to plead facts showing FHEO or City of Boston acted under color of state law. City of Manchester is not an agency of MHRA and took no action relating to the matters at issue. Due process claims regarding voucher termination hearing fail because plaintiff received notice, meaningful opportunity to be heard before neutral decisionmaker, and has not pleaded facts showing she lacked access to records concerning grounds for termination or how earlier access could have changed the result. masked_text: The court granted defendant Flacks' motion to dismiss, finding that Watkins failed to state an Eighth Amendment claim (she is not incarcerated), failed to state ADA or Rehabilitation Act claims against a federal employee, and that sovereign immunity barred her retaliation claim. Ida Watkins, a pro se Section 8 tenant with physical [CLASS], sued her landlord, Metro Housing Boston, and a HUD employee (Flacks) alleging Eighth Amendment deliberate indifference, [CLASS] discrimination under the ADA and Rehabilitation Act, and retaliation for complaining about housing conditions and requesting a shower bar. The court granted Flacks' motion to dismiss, finding no Eighth Amendment claim (Watkins is not incarcerated), no viable ADA claim against a federal employee, no Rehabilitation Act claim (no allegation she sought services from HUD), and sovereign immunity barred the retaliation claim. The court dismissed the FHA [CLAIM] claim against Flacks (a HUD employee) because the complaint failed to allege that Watkins sought services from Flacks or HUD. The complaint alleged discrimination by the landlord and Metro Housing Boston, with no factual allegations that Flacks refused any [CLAIM] request or discriminated in provision of services based on [CLASS]. 12(b)(1) The retaliation claim against Flacks was dismissed on jurisdictional grounds due to sovereign immunity. Although the plaintiffs attempted to revive this claim on appeal by arguing that the Sprinkler Law discriminates because it exempts certain structures (family homes, fraternity houses, dormitories, rest homes, and licensed group homes), the appellate court found the argument underdeveloped and waived. 12(b)(6) The district court dismissed the [CLAIM] claim under Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to state a plausible claim. source_file: 10622451_2025_Gilbert v. Tucson Realty _ Trust Company Management Services LLC_azd
case_name: Shenoa Gilbert v. Tucson Realty & Trust Company Management Services LLC
masked_text: Plaintiff failed to adequately plead the elements of her [CLAIM] claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B) because she did not sufficiently allege how her back injury and kidney disease substantially limit major life activities, that defendant knew of her [CLASS], or how the denial deprived her of equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling. Shenoa Gilbert, a Section 8 voucher holder with a back injury and Stage 3 kidney disease, sued her property management company alleging violations of the Fair Housing Amendments Act and Rehabilitation Act for denying her [CLAIM] requests for a first-floor unit and exemption from pesticide use. The Court dismissed the complaint with leave to amend, finding plaintiff failed to sufficiently plead the elements of her [CLAIM] and retaliation claims. Plaintiff failed to allege how her back injury and kidney disease substantially limit major life activities (element 1), failed to clearly allege she informed defendant of her [CLASS] (element 2), failed to allege how denial of first-floor unit deprived her of equal opportunity to use/enjoy dwelling (element 3), and failed to allege defendant knew or should have known of her [CLASS]. Although plaintiff demonstrated the accommodations were facially reasonable (element 4) and that defendant refused them (element 5), the complaint failed to satisfy all five elements of the [CLAIM] claim under Dubois. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) — Failure to State a Claim Plaintiff failed to allege how her allergies and kidney disease substantially limit major life activities (element 1), failed to clearly allege she informed defendant of her [CLASS] (element 2), and failed to clearly allege that exemption from pesticides was necessary to afford equal opportunity to use/enjoy dwelling (element 3). Although the [CLAIM] appeared facially reasonable and defendant refused it, the complaint did not satisfy all five elements of the [CLAIM] claim. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) — Failure to State a Claim Under 42 U.S.C. § 3617, plaintiff must allege: (1) protected activity, (2) adverse housing consequence causally linked to that activity, and (3) resulting damage. While plaintiff plausibly alleged protected activity (requesting accommodations) and adverse consequences (lease denial, eviction filing) and damages (emotional/financial harm and risk to Section 8 voucher), she failed to clearly allege the causal nexus between her [CLAIM] requests and the subsequent adverse consequences. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) — Failure to State a Claim Under Section 504, plaintiff must show: (1) she is an individual with a [CLASS], (2) she is otherwise qualified to receive the benefit, (3) she was denied benefits solely by reason of [CLASS], and (4) the program receives federal financial assistance. Plaintiff failed to allege how her back injury and kidney disease substantially limit major life activities (element 1), failed to allege the qualifications necessary to live on the first floor and that she meets them (element 2), failed to allege denial was solely based on [CLASS] (element 3), and failed to allege sufficient facts that defendant receives federal financial assistance (element 4). § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) — Failure to State a Claim

case_name: Brown v. Nationwide Mutual Insurance Company
masked_text: All of plaintiff's claims, including FHA [CLAIM] claims, were dismissed with prejudice as time-barred because the alleged discriminatory conduct occurred in 2016 but plaintiff did not file suit until 2024, well beyond the applicable statutes of limitations. Randy Brown sued Nationwide Mutual Insurance Company eight years after a 2016 water damage claim, alleging violations of the ADA and FHA based on the insurer's failure to provide effective communication accommodations about water remediation procedures. The court dismissed all claims with prejudice as time-barred, finding no basis for statutory tolling or equitable exception. The FHA claim accrued in 2016 when plaintiff knew or had reason to know of Nationwide's alleged denial of his request for effective communication. The two-year FHA statute of limitations expired before plaintiff filed suit in 2024. No continuing violation was adequately pleaded, and no tolling applied. Statute of Limitations The FHA hostile environment claim based on alleged misrepresentations in 2016 is barred by the two-year FHA statute of limitations. Plaintiff's allegations of ongoing requests from 2016 to 2024 do not establish a continuing violation because the complaint fails to specify the timing, nature, or Nationwide's response to any requests beyond 2016. Statute of Limitations All non-FHA claims accrued in 2016 based on Nationwide's alleged statements to plaintiff. The ADA claim is time-barred under the applicable statute of limitations (three or four years depending on the theory), and D.C. law claims are barred by the three-year limitations period. No statutory tolling or equitable tolling (including the D.C. 'lulling doctrine') applies because plaintiff has not alleged affirmative misconduct or inducement to delay. Statute of Limitations

row_id: RD-PURE|9683510_2024_Haymarket DuPage, LLC v. Village of Itasca_ilnd
source_file: 9683510_2024_Haymarket DuPage, LLC v. Village of Itasca_ilnd
case_name: Haymarket DuPage, LLC v. Village of Itasca
masked_text: The court granted the Fire District's and School District defendants' motions to dismiss for lack of Article III standing because Haymarket's injury—denial of its zoning applications—was not fairly traceable to those defendants' conduct, as the Village Board held exclusive decision-making authority and the opposing defendants merely voiced concerns without a vote or determinative control over the outcome. Haymarket DuPage, LLC, a nonprofit substance abuse treatment provider, purchased a former Holiday Inn in Itasca, Illinois, and spent two years seeking zoning approval from the Village of Itasca to operate a treatment center; after the Village Board unanimously denied the applications, Haymarket sued six defendants under the Fair Housing Act, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and state law. The Fire Protection District and School District defendants (along with Superintendent Benes) moved to dismiss, arguing Haymarket lacked Article III standing to sue them. The court granted the motions, holding that while those defendants vocally opposed the project, the denial was traceable only to the Village Board—the actual decisionmaker—not to the Fire District or School District, who had no vote and no determinative or coercive control over the Board. The court dismissed claims against the Fire District and School District for lack of Article III standing under 12(b)(1) because the alleged injury (denial of zoning applications by the Village Board) was not fairly traceable to the conduct of those defendants. The Fire District and School District were voices in opposition but not decisionmakers; the Village Board had unfettered discretion and made the final decision. The complaint did not allege that the defendants' approval was necessary or that they had determinative or coercive control over the Board's decision. 12(b)(1) Claims under the ADA Title II, Section 504 Rehabilitation Act, and Illinois state law against the Fire District and School District were dismissed for lack of standing on the same traceability grounds as the FHA claims. The court did not reach the merits of these non-FHA claims because the jurisdictional defect (lack of traceability to the defendants' conduct) was fatal. 12(b)(1)

row_id: RD-PURE|9938953_2023_SAMUEL v. THE DELAWARE COUNTY HOUSING AUTHORITY_paed
source_file: 9938953_2023_SAMUEL v. THE DELAWARE COUNTY HOUSING AUTHORITY_paed
case_name: Earlando Samuel v. The Delaware County Housing Authority
masked_text: The court denied Samuel's premature Rule 12(c) motion, granted Ingerman Defendants' motion to dismiss in full, and granted DCHA Defendants' motion in part, allowing only the HUD live-in aide regulation claim (24 C.F.R. § 982.316) to survive because Samuel sufficiently alleged his two-bedroom aide approval was never validly revoked, while dismissing the FHA Section 3617 claim for failure to allege the harassing conduct was connected to his [CLASS]. Pro se plaintiff Earlando Samuel, a 70-year-old man with osteoporosis, degenerative joint disease, and a mild cognitive disorder, sued the Delaware County Housing Authority (DCHA) and Ingerman Property Management, alleging a 'bait-and-switch' scheme that resulted in his two-bedroom Housing Choice Voucher being downgraded to a one-bedroom voucher and his placement in an unsuitable second-floor one-bedroom apartment, followed by a campaign of harassment including unannounced apartment entries and arbitrary rent fluctuations. Plaintiff failed to show that his requests for a variance and other accommodations had any connection to his medical condition, and did not inform the County of his medical condition until March 2023, well after the state court judgment. Without demonstrating a direct linkage between the proposed [CLAIM] and equal opportunity for the [CLASS] person, the FHA failure-to-accommodate claim cannot succeed. There was no indication that defendants exhibited animus toward plaintiff because of his medical conditions, and plaintiff did not allege that he informed the County of his medical condition during the relevant enforcement proceedings. He claimed only that defendants interfered with his FHA rights after he exercised his right to file appeals and participate in zoning hearings, but did not allege that he exercised or advocated for his FHA rights during any proceedings. Motion for Preliminary Injunction Denied For the Equal Protection claim, plaintiff failed to identify highly similar properties receiving more favorable treatment, as he did not demonstrate when comparator structures were built or whether they were grandfathered in. For substantive due process, the County had a rational basis for enforcing the setback requirement, and plaintiff's failure to exhaust state procedures undermined the claim. Cynthia Monterroso, a [CLASS] homeowner whose home was rebuilt through the City's HUD-funded Build-It-Back Program after Hurricane Sandy, sued the City of New York alleging the reconstructed home contained features incompatible with her [CLASS] [CLASS] and that the City failed to provide reasonable accommodations. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the FHA [CLAIM] claim failed because many requests were unrelated to [CLASS], the complaint did not sufficiently allege requested accommodations were reasonable, and Defendants had already made accommodations including installing a lift and ADA-compliant kitchen. Complaint fails to plausibly allege that requested accommodations are necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling, that accommodations are reasonable, or that defendants refused to make them. Many requests are unrelated to [CLASS]; others describe aesthetic or functional preferences rather than [CLASS]-necessitated accommodations. Defendants' allegations that they offered repairs, issued temporary COs, and made alterations (lift, ADA kitchen) contradict the claim of refusal. 12(b)(6) Although complaint alleges intentional discrimination and differential treatment, it lacks sufficient factual allegations showing that defendants' misconduct regarding the home was motivated by discriminatory animus because of plaintiff's [CLASS]. Conclusory allegations of intentional discrimination are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly. 12(b)(6) ADA/Rehabilitation Act claims fail because complaint does not allege discrimination because of [CLASS] but rather challenges adequacy of housing services provided. Under Tardif and Doe, the ADA prohibits discrimination because of [CLASS], not inadequate treatment for [CLASS]. Due Process claim fails because no final CO denial is alleged and temporary COs were issued. Equal Protection 'class of one' claim fails due to conclusory allegations without identifying specific comparators or explaining identical circumstances. Punitive damages against municipalities are unavailable absent express statutory authorization. 12(b)(6)

row_id: RD-PURE|11267617 - MILLERBORG v. BLUE BONNET TRAIL LLC
source_file: 11267617 - MILLERBORG v. BLUE BONNET TRAIL LLC
case_name: Millerborg v. Blue Bonnet Trail LLC
masked_text: A plaintiff asserting claims about physical accessibility must at least have personally experienced an accessibility issue to have standing; merely observing accessibility barriers without any direct personal effect is insufficient to plead a concrete injury in fact. Casey Millerborg, a [CLASS] user, sued Blue Bonnet Trail LLC, owner of an apartment complex in Waxahachie, Texas, alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on physical accessibility barriers he observed at the property. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss for lack of Article III standing, finding the complaint failed to allege sufficient facts showing Millerborg personally experienced any accessibility barriers rather than merely observing them, and failed to establish likelihood of future injury sufficient for injunctive relief. Plaintiff lacked Article III standing because his complaint failed to allege concrete injury in fact. Although plaintiff visited the property and observed accessibility barriers, he did not sufficiently allege that he personally experienced (as opposed to merely observed) any specific accessibility challenges, and his allegations regarding future injury were insufficient because he stated he would only return after remediation, negating any future harm an injunction could remedy. 12(b)(1)

The [CLAIM] does not provide equal opportunity to use and enjoy the home; it merely seeks to avoid compliance with facially neutral HOA regulations. masked_text: The court recommended dismissal because the WIN Defendants lacked authority over housing placement decisions—DHS retained that authority—so plaintiff's injuries lacked traceability to the WIN Defendants; additionally, plaintiff's demand for transgender-only housing was not adequately tied to her [CLASS]. The complaint alleges DHS controlled shelter placement and rejected the [CLAIM] request, not the WIN Defendants. Additionally, Plaintiff failed to allege a nexus between her alleged [CLASS] and the requested [CLAIM] of living only with transgender individuals, as opposed to the medically-supported need for a private room. 12(b)(6) ADA Title III claim dismissed because DHS, not WIN Defendants, controlled placement and rejected [CLAIM]. NYSHRL and NYCHRL claims fail for same reasons as FHA claim and because Local Law 3 does not require creation of new transgender-only facilities. § 1983 claims fail because WIN Defendants are private entities not acting under color of state law; DHS retained placement authority. Title VI claim fails because no allegation that WIN Defendants received federal funds or discriminated based on [CLASS], color, or national origin. § 504 Rehabilitation Act claim fails for same reasons as ADA claim. 12(b)(6) and 12(b)(1) Plaintiff lacks Article III standing against WIN Defendants because she failed to establish a sufficient causal nexus between WIN Defendants' conduct and her alleged injuries. Although homelessness is a concrete injury, Plaintiff did not allege that WIN Defendants had authority to transfer her or that they possessed transgender-specific housing. Redressability also fails because monetary damages against WIN Defendants would not result in DHS providing the requested [CLAIM], and Plaintiff seeks to hold WIN responsible for DHS's independent conduct. 12(b)(1)

source_file: 11267621 - Gilbert v. TUCSON REALTY & TRUST COMPANY

masked_text: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHAA [CLAIM] claim because her complaint failed to allege sufficient facts showing her [CLASS] substantially limits major life activities, that defendant knew of her [CLASS], and that the [CLAIM] was necessary to afford her equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling. Implications of anaphylactic reaction do not clearly state a claim upon which relief can be granted. 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) Plaintiff adequately alleged protected activity (requesting accommodations) and adverse housing consequences (lease denial, eviction filing) and damages, but failed to clearly allege the causal nexus between her [CLAIM] requests and defendant's subsequent adverse actions. masked_text: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA and ADA claims for failure to state a claim because they contained only conclusory statements without factual allegations explaining what discriminatory actions occurred or what reasonable accommodations were required. case_name: Randy Dewayne Pittman v. Landsphere Property Management, et al.
masked_text: The court dismissed the plaintiff's FHA claim with prejudice for failure to state a claim after the plaintiff failed to file an amended complaint, and dismissed the state-law claims without prejudice for lack of supplemental jurisdiction. Pro se plaintiff Randy Dewayne Pittman sued his landlord and property manager under the FHA and California state law, alleging they failed to create an accessible parking space at his apartment building. The court had previously dismissed his complaint with leave to amend after screening it pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2), finding it failed to state an FHA claim. Because Pittman did not file an amended complaint by the December 1, 2025 deadline, the court dismissed the federal FHA claim with prejudice and the state-law claims without prejudice. The court screened the complaint under § 1915(e)(2) and determined that the FHA claim failed to state a plausible claim. The complaint was dismissed with leave to amend, and upon plaintiff's failure to file an amended complaint by the deadline, the case was dismissed with prejudice. 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2) The court determined that the complaint failed to articulate an independent basis for subject-matter jurisdiction over the state-law claims and declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction, dismissing those claims without prejudice. Supplemental jurisdiction declined

masked_text: The magistrate judge recommended dismissal with prejudice because plaintiff's third complaint was so verbose, confused, and redundant it disguised the true substance of his claims, and despite multiple opportunities to amend and specific guidance from the court, plaintiff persisted in noncompliance with Rule 8 pleading standards. The magistrate judge recommended granting defendants' motion to dismiss with prejudice because plaintiff's third amended complaint was a 72-page, single-spaced, confusing document that failed to comply with Rule 8 despite multiple court orders and opportunities to amend, and the court never reached the merits of any [CLAIM] or discrimination claim. The complaint was dismissed for failure to comply with Rule 8 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and prior court orders. The complaint was so verbose, confused, and redundant that its true substance was disguised, preventing the court from identifying the specific claims asserted. The plaintiff was afforded multiple opportunities to amend and was warned that noncompliance could result in dismissal. Rule 8 / Failure to Comply with Court Orders The complaint was dismissed for failure to comply with Rule 8 and prior court orders. The court could not discern the specific factual allegations supporting discrimination claims due to the complaint's prolix and confusing presentation. Rule 8 / Failure to Comply with Court Orders The complaint was dismissed for failure to comply with Rule 8 and prior court orders. Additionally, the court noted that 18 U.S.C. § 241 and § 242 are criminal statutes that do not provide a private cause of action, and the § 1983 claims lacked sufficiently specific factual allegations and improperly referenced generic 'Defendants and their Agents' without specifying which defendants were at fault. Rule 8 / Failure to Comply with Court Orders
